briefing: Research activity is converging on interface, defect, and strain engineering to make 2D materials more programmable for semiconductors, memory, photonics, and neuromorphic hardware. Reported advances emphasize controllable polarity, analog conductance, multiband transport, polarization-defined emission, and electrically tunable spin effects. Translation remains early-stage: a flash-memory review identifies wafer-scale synthesis, device variability, reliability, and array integration as central barriers. Separately, graphene-derived adsorbents show potential in industrial wastewater treatment, while GMG’s financing signals continued corporate support for graphene activities.

articles.title_original: Selenium Vacancy‐Enabled 2D Bi 2 O 2 Se Optoelectronic Synapses for Neuromorphic Vision Processing
articles.title_en: Selenium Vacancies Enable Neuromorphic Vision Synapses in Bi₂O₂Se
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Neuromorphic visual computing aims to fuse sensing, memory, and processing into a single hardware stack, enabling reliable analog weight updates. Defect engineering in two‐dimensional (2D) semiconductors is an effective strategy for achieving such synaptic functionality. However, in most 2D materials, the defects that confer plasticity also compromise lattice stability and degrade intrinsic performance. This work demonstrates that Bi 2 O 2 Se provides a robust, defect‐tolerant platform. The growth process introduces selenium vacancy (V Se ) without compromising covalent structure or the approximately 0.8 eV bandgap, yielding stable and programmable trap centers. Combined with a low‐trap hexagonal boron nitride (h‐BN) gate dielectric that suppresses extra interfacial states, the resulting Bi 2 O 2 Se/h‐BN transistor exhibits analog conductance modulation, excitatory postsynaptic currents, double‐pulse facilitation, and long‐term potentiation/inhibition, supporting hybrid electro‐optic learning via vacancy‐assisted charge trapping and persistent photoconductivity. Mapping measured device characteristics onto designed convolutional neural networks achieves 90.1% accuracy in complex image recognition, establishing an optoelectrical neuromorphic multifunctional platform for edge intelligence systems.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed selenium-vacancy-engineered Bi₂O₂Se/h-BN transistors with programmable analog conductance and synaptic learning behaviors. The devices achieved 90.1% image-recognition accuracy when mapped to convolutional neural networks, highlighting potential for edge-intelligence hardware.

articles.title_original: Electrostatic and Radio Frequency Performance Optimization of a Triple Metal Gate Hybrid Nanowire Metal Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor
articles.title_en: Simulated Triple-Metal-Gate Nanowire MOSFET Targets High-Speed RF Performance
articles.excerpt_original: This paper presents a simulated study on a 2D Asymmetric Gate Stack-Triple Metal Gate-All-Around (AGS-TM-GAA) Nanowire MOSFET with a SiGe-Ge-InGaAs hybrid channel, multi-work function metal gates, and optimally structured high-k dielectric stack (TiO2/Hf O2/Si3N4). The device has lightly p-doped source/drain, the highly n-doped channel and gate work functions 4.0 eV, 3.9 eV, 4.4 eV to have a greater threshold voltage stability, to lower the potential barriers and to have a better carrier injection. This has been demonstrated to be excellent electrostatic integrity, with steep conduction-band bending ≈-1.5 eV, uniform distribution of fields in the mid-channel ≈1.3-1.5x106 V/m and constant electron mobility ≈8-10 cm2/Vs with ATLAS simulator. The proposed device has the following highest gate-to-drain and gate-coupling capacitances Cgd ≈ 7.5x10-4-2.4x10-3 fF/µm and Cgg ≈ 4.8×10⁻³ fF/µm, maximum drive current Ids ≈ 5x10-3 A, subthreshold slope 2.2x10-4-1.45x10-3 mV/dec and drain conductance ~1x10-3 µS/nm. Short-channel effects, including the variation in threshold-voltage, and degradation of mobility and enhancement of leakage, are substantially reduced due to the GAA, asymmetric gate stack and enhanced quantum confinement. Cut-off frequency (ft), robust FTP behaviour and peak current density are high-frequency metrics that verify the suitability of the architecture to high-speed and Radio Frequency applications.
articles.summary_en: A simulated asymmetric gate-stack, triple-metal-gate, gate-all-around nanowire MOSFET using a SiGe–Ge–InGaAs hybrid channel demonstrates improved electrostatic control, reduced short-channel effects, and stable carrier injection. articles.title_original: Reducing Hydrogen Diffusion Losses by Modification of Fluoroplastic Barrier Coatings for Increasing Efficiency and Safety of Hydrogen Transportation
articles.title_en: Nanomodified PTFE Coatings Reduce Hydrogen Permeation in Steel Pipelines
articles.excerpt_original: High pressure hydrogen transport can cause hydrogen embrittlement of steel pipelines, leading to loss of mechanical integrity and failures. Therefore, protective internal coatings are required to reduce hydrogen permeability. In this work, the effect of composite fluoropolymer coatings modified with carbon nanotubes (CNTs), silicon carbide (SiC), and hexagonal boron nitride (h BN) on the hydrogen permeability of 1020 steel was studied using the Devanathan–Stachurski electrochemical method. The effective diffusion coefficient, steady state diffusion flux, and hydrogen concentration in the near surface layer were determined for uncoated steel, steel with a graphite layer, and various nanomodified PTFE coatings. Applying fluoropolymer coatings containing CNTs significantly reduced the effective diffusion coefficient and hydrogen flux compared to uncoated steel. Additional incorporation of SiC and h BN particles enabled further tailoring of the barrier properties. The PTFE based composition filled with CNTs and SiC provided the lowest effective diffusion coefficient and diffusion flux, which is attributed to the formation of a dense, low defect polymer structure with an elongated diffusion path. To evaluate the influence of the nanofiller composition on agglomeration and coating defectiveness, the ratio of reduction coefficients ηJ/ηD is proposed as an additional performance indicator. Diffusion loss calculations for a model pipeline section showed that the developed coatings substantially reduce hydrogen permeation through the steel wall, confirming their potential for internal pipeline protection in hydrogen transport and storage systems.
articles.summary_en: Researchers found that PTFE coatings containing carbon nanotubes and silicon carbide substantially reduced hydrogen diffusion and flux through 1020 steel. The coatings could improve protection of pipelines and storage systems against hydrogen embrittlement and permeation losses.

articles.title_original: Physics-guided Gaussian process framework for data-efficient optimization of APCVD growth of 2D semiconductor WS2
articles.title_en: Physics-guided machine learning optimizes APCVD growth of WS₂
articles.excerpt_original: Layer-controlled growth of two-dimensional transition-metal dichalcogenides (2D TMDs), such as Tungsten Disulfide (WS 2 ), remains challenging due to the nonlinear interplay among multiple parameters associated with the atmospheric pressure chemical vapor deposition (APCVD) growth technique. In particular, achieving large-area few-layer flakes of TMDs is significantly more challenging than growing bulk using conventional APCVD method. Here, we present a physics-guided Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) framework for data-efficient exploration of the APCVD growth parameter space of WS 2 . An initial database of 12 experimentally measured growths is used to construct a GPR surrogate model, with WS 2 areal flake coverage quantified by optical-image analysis. Virtual candidate conditions are subsequently generated by Monte Carlo sampling and ranked using a composite acquisition score incorporating a domain-guided density target, predictive uncertainty, and standardized parameter-space novelty. Machine Learning (ML) generated candidates are maintained separately from the experimental database and are not used as pseudo-labels for model training. Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) of the 12 experimental observations gives an R 2 of 0.719, mean absolute error (MAE) of 8.23 percentage points, root mean square error (RMSE) of 11.96 percentage points, and Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.854. The framework identifies promising regions of the APCVD parameter space while explicitly quantifying predictive uncertainty. Further, the optical microscopy, Raman spectroscopy, and photoluminescence measurements are used to characterize experimentally obtained WS 2 crystals.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a physics-guided Gaussian process framework to efficiently optimize atmospheric-pressure chemical vapor deposition of large-area, few-layer WS₂. Using 12 experimental growths, the model identified promising process conditions and quantified uncertainty, with follow-up optical, Raman, and photoluminescence characterization.

articles.title_original: Narrow-Line-Width Electroluminescence in Monolayer WSe2 Enabled by a Sub-5 nm Au/Pt Nanogap
articles.title_en: Sub-5 nm Au/Pt Nanogap Enables Narrow-Linewidth WSe2 Electroluminescence
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Spectrally isolated, electrically driven emission from localized states in two-dimensional semiconductors remains challenging in scalable planar devices. Here, we report narrow-line-width alternating-current electroluminescence (ACEL) from localized states in monolayer WSe2 using a lithographically defined sub-5 nm Au/Pt nanogap on SiO2/Si at 3.5 K. The curved nanogap geometry produces a nonuniform strain landscape and regions of enhanced electric field that may influence the local electronic environment. Under square-wave gate excitation, the device exhibits a spectrally isolated ACEL line at 1.652 eV with an apparent fitted line width of approximately 2 meV, in contrast to broad, multipeak photoluminescence from the same device. Spectral decomposition identifies dominant ZPL-like and weaker red-shifted sideband-like contributions. This nanogap architecture provides a scalable planar platform for narrow-line-width, electrically driven localized emission in two-dimensional materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated electrically driven, spectrally isolated electroluminescence from localized states in monolayer WSe2 using a lithographically defined sub-5 nm Au/Pt nanogap. The platform produced an approximately 2 meV emission line at 3.5 K, indicating potential for scalable planar devices based on two-dimensional semiconductors.

articles.title_original: Highly Controllable Polarity in Two-Dimensional Vertical Transistors
articles.title_en: Graphene-Enabled Vertical MoTe₂ Transistors Achieve Controllable Polarity
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Two-dimensional (2D) vertical transistors, featuring atomically thin channels and an inherent vertical architecture, hold extensive promise for ultrascaled electronics. However, achieving reliable polarity control in such devices has remained a persistent challenge over the past decade. Here, we demonstrate a vertical MoTe2 transistor with highly controllable polarity. By implementing van der Waals (vdW) integration for both contacts, the carrier injection barrier can be effectively modulated via the work functions of the electrodes. Leveraging the favorable band alignment with graphene and the narrow bandgap of MoTe2, we achieve selective n-type and p-type operation using Ag and Pt top contacts, respectively. Furthermore, through graphene work-function engineering, we optimize the switching performance, realizing an on/off ratio exceeding 104 in a ∼5 nm p-type MoTe2 vertical transistor, surpassing all previously reported p-type 2D vertical transistors based on graphene/TMD/metal architectures. Finally, we integrate two vertical transistors of opposite polarities, fabricated from graphene/MoTe2 heterostructure with different top contacts, to demonstrate a complementary inverter on a single chip. Our work not only provides a viable strategy for polarity control in vertical heterostructures but also suggests a potential pathway toward complementary circuits based on 2D vertical transistors.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated graphene/MoTe₂ vertical transistors with selective n-type or p-type operation by varying top-contact materials and engineering graphene work functions. The devices achieved an on/off ratio above 10⁴ and enabled a complementary inverter, highlighting potential for ultrascaled 2D electronics.

articles.title_original: Synergistic Interfacial Confinement and CVD-Derived Graphene Encapsulation in Silicon/Reduced Graphene Oxide/Graphene Composite for High-Performance Si Anodes
articles.title_en: CVD graphene encapsulation improves silicon anode stability
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Silicon (Si)-based anodes are promising for next-generation lithium-ion batteries but suffer from severe volume expansion, structural degradation, and unstable interphase during cycling. Herein, a synergistic oxidation and controllable assembly strategy are proposed. First, Si nanoparticles (SiNPs) are co-oxidized with graphite, during which the SiOx layer formed on the SiNP surface chemically bonds with the oxygen-containing functional groups of graphene oxide (GO) nanosheets. This interaction integrates SiNPs into the three-dimensional (3D) GO network via intercalation, wrapping, and anchoring, yielding a hierarchically encapsulated Si/GO precursor. Subsequently, chemical vapor deposition (CVD) is conducted to grow an outer graphene shell in situ on the Si/GO precursor, ultimately producing the Si/rGO/Gr composite. In this architecture, the 3D GO network provides multilevel buffering spaces, while the outer graphene layer serves as a conductive and mechanical confinement sheath, synergistically mitigating Si expansion and facilitating charge transfer. The optimized Si/rGO/Gr anode delivers reversible capacities of 1104.6 and 678.2 mAh g−1 at 0.05 and 1 A g−1, respectively. When assembled into a full cell with a LiFePO4 cathode, the Si/rGO/Gr anode exhibits reversible capacities of 149.0 and 113.2 mAh g−1 at 0.5 and 5 C, respectively. This work demonstrates that the combination of synergistic oxidation, controllable assembly, and CVD graphene encapsulation offers a viable synthetic route toward high-stability Si-based anodes.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a silicon/reduced graphene oxide/graphene composite anode using interfacial bonding and an in situ CVD-grown graphene shell. The architecture buffers silicon expansion and supports charge transfer, delivering reported reversible capacities of 1104.6 mAh g−1 at 0.05 A g−1 and 678.2 mAh g−1 at 1 A g−1.

articles.title_original: Flexible MXene actuator with multi-stimulus responsiveness for biomimetic motions
articles.title_en: Flexible MXene–PVDF actuator enables multi-stimulus biomimetic robots
articles.excerpt_original: Inspired by soft-bodied organisms in nature, this study fabricated an actuator with asymmetric curvature on its two sides using an unconventional dual-flow filtration method. Owing to the significant difference in the thermal expansion coefficients between MXene and PVDF, MXene serves as the active layer while PVDF acts as the inert layer. This actuator can deform under multiple stimuli, such as light, heat, and electricity, and exhibit excellent stability. Furthermore, by leveraging the differential bending performance of its two sides, a flexible robot capable of crawling under near-infrared light (NIR) irradiation has been developed. This robot demonstrates a relatively fast NIR response time (11.2 s) and recovery time (7.7 s). Furthermore, doping MXene with NiFe 2 O 4 nanoparticles endows the flexible robot with magnetically responsive actuation. Under multi-stimuli control, the composite actuator can crawl through complex paths. Additionally, actuators with such characteristics can be applied to asymmetrically structured flexible grippers. Under a light intensity of 180 mW/cm 2 , the gripper achieves a bending angle of 182°. This work provides an effective strategy for the design and fabrication of flexible actuators and bioinspired intelligent devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a flexible MXene–PVDF actuator responsive to light, heat, and electricity, with added magnetic responsiveness from NiFe₂O₄ nanoparticles. The actuator powered a near-infrared crawling robot and flexible gripper, demonstrating potential for bioinspired soft robotics.

articles.title_original: Quantum Dot One-Dimensional Arrays Using Templates: Recent Progress and Future Perspectives
articles.title_en: Template Strategies for One-Dimensional Quantum-Dot Arrays
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) represent a premier class of inorganic nanomaterials featuring tunable optical properties, including size- and composition-dependent light absorption and photoluminescence (PL). Recent research has focused on their highly ordered 2D and 3D assemblies, termed superlattices, which exhibit collective photophysical phenomena such as long-range exciton diffusion and superfluorescence. However, constructing lower-dimensional architectures, such as 1D arrays capable of directional energy transport, remains a formidable challenge. This difficulty arises because conventional QDs lack the intrinsic shape anisotropy required for anisotropic self-assembly. This Perspective highlights recent progress in fabricating 1D arrays from spherical and cubic QDs, with particular emphasis on rational scaffolding and templating strategies that enable precise structural control. Finally, we provide perspectives on the future design of nanoscale and mesoscale superstructures integrating organic and inorganic nanomaterials.
articles.summary_en: This perspective reviews methods for fabricating ordered one-dimensional arrays from spherical and cubic quantum dots. It highlights scaffolding and templating approaches for controlling nanoscale architectures and enabling directional energy transport.

articles.title_original: Defect-engineered semiconductor nanomaterials for photocatalytic hydrogen evolution: mechanistic insights, design strategies, and future perspectives
articles.title_en: Defect engineering advances photocatalytic hydrogen evolution
articles.excerpt_original: Photocatalytic hydrogen production is an insistent route to solar fuel generation, yet its practical efficiency remains limited by charge recombination, photocorrosion, sluggish interfacial kinetics, and inadequate visible-light harvesting. Defect engineering offers a powerful solution by precisely reshaping semiconductor electronic structures, carrier dynamics, surface reactivity, and reaction pathways. Anion vacancies, cation deficiencies, dopant-induced distortions, and surface disorder can create active states, regulate charge separation, and optimise adsorption energetics across oxides, sulphides, nitrides, and carbon-based photocatalysts. Advances in defect-controlled synthesis and operando characterisation are enabling increasingly rational structure–activity relationships. However, defect instability, synthetic reproducibility, ambiguous defect quantification, inconsistent performance benchmarking, and scale-up remain critical barriers. Future progress demands an integrated paradigm coupling defect engineering with morphology control, heterointerface design, and device-level architectures. Such convergence can transform defect-rich photocatalysts from laboratory-scale materials into durable, high-efficiency platforms for economically viable solar hydrogen production.
articles.summary_en: The review examines how vacancies, dopants, and surface disorder can improve charge separation, visible-light absorption, and reaction kinetics in semiconductor photocatalysts for solar hydrogen production. It identifies defect instability, reproducibility, benchmarking, and scale-up as key barriers to commercialization.

articles.title_original: Design principle for mitigating moisture-induced degradation in 2D halide perovskites
articles.title_en: Branched Spacer Cations Improve Moisture Stability of 2D Perovskites
articles.excerpt_original: We establish a conceptual framework which explains and mitigates moisture-induced degradation in 2D perovskites. Degradation proceeds along defined pathways across the spacer cation iodide (A′I or A′I2)-PbI2-H2O ternary phase diagram as moisture intercalates into the perovskite. Phases evolve as the composition of the system travels towards the H2O and PbI2 sides of the phase diagram. The structure and chemistry of the spacer cations control the availability and formation energies of non-perovskite phases, which in turn determines the degradation mechanism and rate in humid air. In particular, stable 2D perovskites typically can coexist in thermodynamic equilibrium with water, whereas unstable 2D perovskites typically cannot because they are impeded by hydrate phases. This framework establishes a design principle focused on tuning the spacer cation to not accomodate low-energy hydrate phases and other lead-rich phases, thereby suppressing moisture driven degradation and enhancing 2D perovskite stability. Leveraging this mechanism, we show that replacing linear butylammonium with branched isobutylammonium suppresses moisture-induced degradation of the associated 2D powders by a factor of six. The existence of mixed-organic cation non-perovskite phases can similarly destabilize mixed 3D-2D perovskite films, and suppressing such mixed phases improves stability. In humid air, 2D perovskites degrade into various lead-rich nonperovskite phases. The easier it is for such phases to form, the faster degradation proceeds. By tuning a 2D perovskite’s molecular cations to not accommodate any lead-rich phases, stability can be markedly improved.
articles.summary_en: Researchers establish a phase-diagram framework linking spacer-cation chemistry to moisture-driven degradation in 2D halide perovskites. Replacing linear butylammonium with branched isobutylammonium reduced degradation sixfold, highlighting a design route for more stable perovskite devices.

articles.title_original: PtSe2/Graphene Interfacial Coupling Enhances the Intrinsic Electrocatalytic Activity of PtSe2 Edge Sites
articles.title_en: PtSe2/Graphene Coupling Boosts Hydrogen-Evolution Catalysis
articles.excerpt_original: Platinum-based chalcogenides (PtX2) can be efficiently activated as electrocatalysts for water splitting through the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Edges in layered PtSe2 are effective in HER; however, the effect of edge interaction with conductive electrodes like graphene remains unclear. This study investigates the mechanism by which PtX2 (X = S, Se, Te) edges interact with graphene to uncover the origin of chalcogen-dependent differences in electrocatalysis through interfacial electronic coupling. Graphene flakes decorated with PtX2 nanosheets have reduced overpotential and enhanced kinetics in the HER. Interestingly, PtSe2/graphene exhibits the lowest overpotential among all samples, even though it also has the lowest electrochemically accessible surface area. First-principles calculations confirm the interfacial coupling between PtSe2 edges and graphene with pronounced charge accumulation in platinum-selenium edges. Gibbs free energy calculations show different activities for different chalcogens of PtX2/graphene, consistent with experimental results. Our findings indicate that graphene acts as an electronic regulator for PtSe2/graphene, which enhances the intrinsic catalytic activity of the platinum-selenium edge sites, making them more effective for the HER despite their lower density. This interfacial electronic coupling through conductive electrodes provides a powerful strategy for the rational design of next-generation electrocatalysts, enabling enhanced activity and selectivity in advanced electrochemical systems.
articles.summary_en: Academic research shows that interfacial electronic coupling between graphene and PtSe2 edge sites lowers overpotential and improves hydrogen-evolution reaction kinetics. The findings identify graphene as an electronic regulator that can enhance intrinsic electrocatalytic activity despite reduced accessible surface area, supporting catalyst design for water-splitting systems.

articles.title_original: The rise of MXene-based nanofluids as the novel coolants: A state of the art and future perspectives
articles.title_en: MXene Nanofluids Emerge as Advanced Cooling Fluids
articles.excerpt_original: Nanofluids (NFs) represent a promising approach to enhance heat transfer in various systems. However, their translation into practical thermal management systems remains constrained by persistent challenges such as colloidal instability and agglomeration of the particles, viscosity-related hydraulic penalties, fouling and erosion risks in flow passages, and limited reproducibility of thermophysical properties across studies. The recent emergence of MXenes, a diverse family of 2D transition metal carbides, nitrides, and carbonitrides opens novel opportunities for designing next-generation NFs. The colloidal MXene solutions demonstrate remarkable thermal conductivity and superior long-term stability without the need for surfactants, distinguishing them from traditional NF components. This vision article aims to critically assess the current state of MXene-based nanofluids for heat transfer applications and identify structure-property relationships that can guide their rational design. Recent studies demonstrate thermal conductivity enhancements of up to 60–70% in MXene-based nanofluids, while relatively low particle concentrations can provide substantial improvements in convective and boiling heat transfer. Importantly, surface terminations, defect density, oxidation state, flake size, and layer number strongly affect thermal transport, stability, and rheological behavior. At the same time, MXene degradation, insufficient structural characterization, and limited reproducibility remain key barriers to practical implementation. Based on these findings, we outline major research priorities toward scalable, durable, and application-specific MXene-based coolants
articles.summary_en: A review identifies MXene-based nanofluids as promising thermal-management coolants, reporting thermal-conductivity gains of up to 60–70% and improved convective and boiling heat transfer at low concentrations. Practical deployment remains limited by degradation, characterization gaps, reproducibility, viscosity penalties, and flow-channel fouling risks.

articles.title_original: Surface amorphization enables phonon mode activation and enhanced thermal transport at 2D/3D van der Waals heterostructures
articles.title_en: Surface amorphization boosts thermal transport across h-BN interfaces
articles.excerpt_original: Efficient heat dissipation across van der Waals (vdW) interfaces between two-dimensional (2D) materials and three-dimensional (3D) substrates remains a fundamental bottleneck in nanoelectronic devices. Here, using molecular dynamics simulations, we demonstrate that introducing an atomically thin amorphous layer on the substrate surface dramatically enhances interfacial thermal transport at the hexagonal boron nitride/silicon dioxide (h-BN/SiO₂) interface. The interfacial thermal conductance increases by up to ~2.8 × compared with a smooth crystalline surface and can be further tuned by substrate roughness, interfacial coupling strength, and vacancy concentration. Spectral heat current and phonon mode analyses reveal a previously unexplored mechanism whereby amorphous surface topology activates intermediate and localized phonon modes, enabling efficient coupling between in-plane and out-of-plane phonons in h-BN and facilitating energy transfer into the substrate. This process redistributes high-frequency phonons toward low-frequency heat-carrying modes, induces a blueshift of acoustic phonons, and shortens phonon lifetimes through symmetry breaking and nonuniform vdW interactions. Our results establish surface amorphization as an effective and experimentally accessible strategy for engineering phonon transport at 2D/3D vdW interfaces, offering new opportunities for thermal management in 2D material-based nanoelectronics.
articles.summary_en: Molecular dynamics simulations show that an atomically thin amorphous layer on SiO₂ can increase interfacial thermal conductance with h-BN by up to 2.8×. The mechanism activates intermediate phonon modes and could improve heat dissipation in 2D nanoelectronic devices.

articles.title_original: Strong Light-Matter Interactions in 2D Materials
articles.title_en: Study Reveals Tunable Exciton-Polariton Behavior in 2D Semiconductors
articles.excerpt_original: Integrating 2D materials into high-quality optical microcavities opens the door to fascinating many-particle phenomena, including the formation of exciton-polaritons. These are hybrid quasi-particles inheriting properties of both the constituent photons and excitons. The corresponding change in the dispersion relation has a large impact on the optics, dynamics and transport behaviour of the materials. In this thesis, we aim to microscopically understand the optical response and propagation of exciton-polaritons in transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs). The theoretical method is based on the density matrix formalism combined with the Hopfield approach. In particular, we investigate how the exciton diffusion changes in the strong coupling regime, i.e. when exciton-polaritons are formed. Furthermore, we study the impact of dark excitons on the optical response of upper and lower polariton branches in absorption spectra of molybdenum- and tungsten-based TMDs, which are known to be direct and indirect semiconductors, respectively. We show how different experimentally accessible quantities, such as temperature or mirror reflectance, can be exploited to tune the optical response of polaritons. By changing the cavity detuning, we vary the polariton energy relative to the unaffected dark excitons in such a way that we open or close specific phonon-driven scattering channels. In a joint theory-experiment, with the group of Christian Schneider (University of Oldenburg), we show that this controlled switching of scattering channels manifests in characteristic sharp changes in the optical spectra of polaritons. These spectral features can be exploited to extract the position of dark excitons. This suggests new possibilities for exploiting polaritons for fingerprinting nanomaterial
articles.summary_en: A thesis examines strong light–matter interactions in transition metal dichalcogenides within optical microcavities. It shows that cavity detuning can control phonon-driven scattering channels and enable dark-exciton identification through optical spectra.

articles.title_original: Decoupling Thermal and Electronic Effects of Metal Contacts in Bilayer MoS2 Transistors
articles.title_en: Low-Melting Metals Improve MoS2 Transistor Contacts
articles.excerpt_original: Contact resistance remains a primary bottleneck in two-dimensional (2D) semiconductor field-effect transistors (FETs), yet the concurrent influence of metal work function, adhesion, and deposition temperature obscures the underlying mechanisms. Here, using bilayer MoS2 as a model system, we systematically benchmark four metals (In, Bi, Ti, Pd) and discover that the metal melting point, which sets the deposition thermal budget, is strongly correlated with interface integrity. Low-melting-point metals (Bi, In) preserve an intact van der Waals gap (≈0.3 nm), whereas high-melting-point metals (Ti, Pd) damage the interface and collapse the gap to ≈0.19 nm (Pd) or destroy it entirely (Ti), as revealed by high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM). Despite Fermi-level pinning rendering all devices n-type, Pd outperforms Ti in contact resistance, underscoring the primacy of interface quality over work function alignment. Remarkably, Bi, despite its higher melting point and work function than In, delivers the lowest contact resistance (≈0.14 kΩ·μm) and highest on-state current (≈525 μA·μm-1 at Lch = 100 nm), which we attribute to its semi-metallic band structure that suppresses metal-induced gap states. This work establishes a design rule of contact metals for n-type MoS2 FETs: low work function, low deposition temperature, and low density of states, which is expected to extend to other 2D semiconductor nanoelectronics and integrated circuits.
articles.summary_en: Researchers show that deposition thermal budget and interface integrity strongly affect contact resistance in bilayer MoS2 transistors. Bismuth delivered the best reported performance, supporting low-work-function, low-temperature, low-density-of-states metals for 2D semiconductor electronics.

articles.title_original: Ramp-up performance measurement in job–shop systems using real-time location data: a case study in semiconductor manufacturing
articles.title_en: Real-Time Location Tracking Improves Semiconductor Production Ramp-Up
articles.excerpt_original: Production ramp-up is traditionally characterized by instability, unpredictability, and complexity. Industry 4.0 is changing the future of ramp-up management by facilitating the quantification of early-stage ramp-up performance and enabling manufacturers to accelerate their ramp-up. This work contributes to ramp-up manufacturing by (i) introducing a performance measurement framework specifically designed for job–shop environments and (ii) developing and implementing a low-cost, scalable real-time location system (RTLS) architecture that tracks the real-time positions of products on the shop floor. The effectiveness of the framework is demonstrated through a real-world deployment at a photonic semiconductor foundry undergoing ramp-up. Results indicate that the framework can quantitatively assess the progress of production toward regular operations. Moreover, the RTLS captures valuable information—such as actual production pathways and traceability—that conventional Work-In-Progress (WIP) tracking systems are unable to provide.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed and deployed a low-cost real-time location system and performance framework for measuring ramp-up in a photonic semiconductor foundry. The system provides production-pathway and traceability data beyond conventional work-in-progress tracking, supporting more effective transition to regular operations.

articles.title_original: Symmetry Engineering Enables Deterministic Ensemble Polarization Control in Hexagonal Boron Nitride
articles.title_en: Strain Engineering Aligns h-BN Quantum Emitters for Deterministic Polarization Control
articles.excerpt_original: Optical polarization is a key degree of freedom in quantum photonic and sensing technologies, enabling efficient light--matter coupling and directional emission. However, in defect ensemble-based quantum systems, orientational averaging across many defects suppresses optical anisotropy and eliminates a deterministic polarization axis. Here, symmetry engineering is introduced as a strategy to restore collective optical anisotropy in negatively charged boron vacancy (V_B^-) ensembles hosted in hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN). By imposing anisotropic in-plane tensile strain through lithographically defined nano-ridge arrays, in-plane symmetry is broken and the ensemble emission dipole is aligned with the ridge-defined strain symmetry axis. Polarization-resolved photoluminescence reveals that the polarization visibility scales with the magnitude of strain anisotropy, while the emission orientation rigidly follows the engineered symmetry axis across devices with varying strain direction. This deterministic alignment is independent of crystal orientation, establishing the optical foundation for polarization-defined ensemble spin readout and programmable photonic integration in two-dimensional quantum materials
articles.summary_en: Researchers used lithographically defined nano-ridge arrays to impose anisotropic strain in hexagonal boron nitride, aligning emission from boron-vacancy ensembles along a programmable axis. The approach could support polarization-defined spin readout and integrated photonic devices.

articles.title_original: Graphene-Integrated One-Dimensional Photonic Crystal for Enhanced Optical Biosensing: A Transfer-Matrix Study
articles.title_en: Graphene-integrated photonic crystal model advances optical biosensor design
articles.excerpt_original: Graphene-assisted one-dimensional photonic crystals provide a route for controlling electromagnetic confinement at a sensing interface while retaining the compact geometry of multilayer optical sensors. This manuscript develops a transfer-matrix-based description of a graphene-integrated 1D photonic-crystal biosensor consisting of a BK7 coupling prism, dielectric/graphene periodic layers, a thin plasmonic metal film, an interfacial binding layer, and an aqueous sensing medium. The supplied simulation study compares conventional SPR, photonic-crystal, PC-SPR, and glass-assisted PC-SPR arrangements for Au, Ag, and Cu. Calculations are performed for TM-polarized illumination at 633 nm. For the Au case, the model uses a 45 nm metal film, a 0.34 nm graphene layer, a 470 nm PMMA layer, a 3 nm binding layer, and nine periodic units. The reported angular spectra indicate that incorporation of the photonic-crystal/glass section narrows the resonance feature. The literature source used in the supplied report also describes a 14.8-fold sensitivity enhancement for a graphene-based 1D photonic-crystal sensor; this value is a literature result and is not presented here as a new experimental measurement. The study therefore provides a reproducible numerical framework for subsequent optimization and experimental validation.
articles.summary_en: A transfer-matrix study models graphene-integrated one-dimensional photonic-crystal biosensors combining dielectric layers, plasmonic metals and an aqueous sensing interface. Simulations indicate narrower resonances, while a reported 14.8-fold sensitivity improvement is attributed to prior literature rather than new experimental validation.

articles.title_original: Control of Electronic Properties of Organic–Inorganic MXenes via Surface Functionalization
articles.title_en: Surface Functionalization Tunes MXene Electronic Properties Across Eight Orders of Magnitude
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Surface terminations critically affect the electronic structure of two-dimensional (2D) transition metal carbides and nitrides (MXenes), yet the synthetic exploration has been hindered by the lack of predictive factors. Here, we establish that the number of lone-pair electrons (LPEs) on an organic ligand serves as a key factor governing the synthesis of organic-inorganic hybrid MXenes. Experimentally, successful surface functionalization is strongly dominated by 3-LPE ligands, enabling the synthesis of a broad library of over 20 distinct organically terminated MXenes (OT-MXenes). DFT calculations on representative experimentally realized terminations further show that the investigated 3-LPE ligands preferentially stabilize highly coordinated FCC configurations, providing a microscopic connection between LPE availability, surface coordination, and the experimentally observed functionalization behavior. Remarkably, organic surface termination enables the intrinsic carrier density of MXenes to be tuned over 7-8 orders of magnitude. This unprecedented level of control provides access to the intrinsically high carrier mobility in the low-carrier-density regime. In particular, hexanamide-terminated Ti3C2 exhibits an electron mobility of ∼48 cm2 V–1 s–1, representing an improvement of more than two orders of magnitude compared to metallic Ti3C2Tx. Our work clarifies a fundamental design principle for MXene surface engineering, which may guide the precise synthesis of organic-inorganic hybrid MXenes with tailored terminations and properties, thereby promoting MXene device applications and advancing the development of organic-inorganic 2D materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers identified lone-pair electron count as a key factor in synthesizing organically terminated MXenes, producing more than 20 hybrid materials. Hexanamide-terminated Ti3C2 achieved approximately 48 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ electron mobility, demonstrating major potential for tunable 2D electronic devices.

articles.title_original: Local Metasurface With Vertically Stacked III‐V Semiconductor Disks for Resonant Nonlinear Optics and Up‐Conversion Imaging
articles.title_en: Vertically Stacked AlGaAs Metasurface Enables Resonant Up-Conversion Imaging
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT III‐V semiconductor metasurfaces are promising platforms for realizing sub‐wavelength‐scale frequency converters due to their superior linear and nonlinear optical properties. Here, we report strong resonant enhancement in nonlinear optical processes from a novel semiconductor metasurface consisting of arrays of vertically stacked AlGaAs disks held together by a thin GaAs stem. The metasurface supports highly localized resonances due to the excitation of hybrid anapole scattering modes among closely spaced disks within the vertical stack. Linear reflectance studies on the fabricated metasurfaces show characteristic resonance dips due to anapole‐like scattering mode which agrees with the peak in the second harmonic (SHG) and sum frequency generation (SFG). Strong resonant enhancement in SHG and SFG are achieved with intensity normalized conversion efficiencies as high as 1 × 10 −3 (1.9 × 10 −5 ) and 1.55 × 10 −4 (2.05 × 10 −5 ) cm 2 /GW under widefield (tightly focussed) excitation, respectively. The conversion efficiency numbers obtained here are comparable with some of the highest reported under pulsed excitation, despite the metasurface having significantly lower quality factor (∼20). As an application of the resonant frequency conversion process, we demonstrate widefield up‐conversion imaging by frequency converting extended object patterns imprinted on the incident beam to shorter wavelengths which are imaged using conventional silicon‐based camera with good up‐conversion image quality.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a III–V semiconductor metasurface made from vertically stacked AlGaAs disks joined by GaAs stems, producing enhanced second-harmonic and sum-frequency generation through hybrid anapole modes. The platform enabled widefield up-conversion imaging with a conventional silicon camera, indicating potential for compact nonlinear optical imaging systems.

articles.title_original: Can Organic and Oxide Semiconductors Do More Than Coexist? Functional Heterointerfaces for Hybrid Thin‐Film Transistors
articles.title_en: Organic–oxide heterointerfaces enable multifunctional thin-film transistors
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Organic and oxide semiconductors differ fundamentally in their transport physics, interfacial chemistry, mechanical behavior, and processing requirements, yet these differences also make them functionally complementary. Integrating the two material classes, however, remains challenging because of their distinct surface chemistries, deposition conditions, thermal budgets, and interfacial stability. Beyond the question of whether such dissimilar materials can simply coexist, a more important issue is whether their integration can create functions unavailable to either material alone. This review demonstrates how carefully engineered organic‐oxide heterointerfaces can transform material dissimilarity into a functional advantage, enabling sensing, memory, nonlinear signal processing, and computation. We classify hybridization at the circuit, channel, and interface‐layer levels and connect each architecture to its underlying charge‐injection, transfer, trapping, recombination, tunneling, and fluctuation mechanisms. Lateral and vertically stacked circuits exploit the natural polarity matching between p‐type organic and n‐type oxide semiconductors, whereas directly coupled or interlayer‐mediated channels enable ambipolar, anti‐ambipolar, negative‐transconductance, Gaussian‐like, and sigmoidal responses. Hybrid contact, dielectric, passivation, and charge‐storage layers further regulate injection barriers, molecular organization, photogating, and carrier retention. By linking hybrid architecture and interface coupling to device transfer functions and target applications, this review presents organic‐oxide heterointerfaces as a design platform for thin‐film transistors and heterojunction devices.
articles.summary_en: A review finds that engineered organic–oxide semiconductor interfaces can combine complementary transport and processing characteristics to enable sensing, memory, nonlinear signal processing, and computation. Hybrid architectures and interface layers regulate charge injection, trapping, recombination, tunneling, and carrier retention in thin-film transistor and heterojunction devices.

articles.title_original: Strain-Switchable Piezovalley States in Janus Altermagnetic V2AsHO
articles.title_en: Strain-switchable piezovalley states identified in Janus altermagnetic semiconductor
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Altermagnets enable momentum-dependent spin splitting without net magnetization, but coupling such spin-split electronic states to switchable valley and electromechanical degrees of freedom remains largely unexplored. Here, using first-principles calculations, we identify Janus monolayer V2AsHO as a two-dimensional altermagnetic semiconductor hosting strain-switchable piezovalley states. The compensated antiferromagnetic ground state exhibits pronounced momentum-dependent spin splitting, consistent with altermagnetic order. Owing to the broken out-of-plane mirror symmetry of the Janus lattice, V2AsHO possesses a finite out-of-plane piezoelectric response. More importantly, uniaxial strain lifts the degeneracy between the X and Y valleys and reversibly switches the valley polarization, whereas biaxial strain largely preserves their equivalence. Carrier doping under uniaxial strain further induces a piezomagnetic response, linking the strain-induced valley imbalance to magneto-electromechanical functionality. Polarization-dependent optical absorption exhibits a strain-dependent anisotropy correlated with the piezovalley state.
articles.summary_en: First-principles calculations identify monolayer V2AsHO as an altermagnetic semiconductor whose valley polarization can be reversibly switched by uniaxial strain. The predicted piezoelectric, piezomagnetic and polarization-dependent optical responses suggest potential for strain-controlled semiconductor and optoelectronic devices.

articles.title_original: Integration of hBN Single‐Photon Emitters Into a Hybrid Optomechanical Membrane‐In‐The‐Middle Fiber‐Cavity
articles.title_en: hBN Single-Photon Emitters Integrated with Fiber-Cavity Optomechanics
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT The integration of membranes into optical resonators plays a key role in a variety of applications, including optomechanics. Membranes hosting single photon emitters, ideally with access to spin states, open new roads toward (spin‐) optomechanics. Hexagonal boron nitride is among the most promising two‐dimensional materials showing excellent optical and mechanical properties combined with the ability to host optical active (spin‐) defects. The deterministic creation of optically active defect centers in hexagonal boron nitride membranes and their coupling to optomechanical systems is an outstanding challenge. Here, we explore an alternative, hybrid approach in order to establish coupling between a single photon emitter in commercially available hexagonal boron nitride flakes and a fiber‐cavity mode. We solve technical challenges, such as scattering losses arising from an uncontrolled flake topography. We extend our work by positioning the single photon emitter in hexagonal boron nitride flakes on a highly strained silicon nitride membrane in a membrane‐in‐the‐middle configuration. The mechanical vibrational modes of the silicon nitride membrane and cavity‐coupled emission from the single photon emitter are simultaneously observed. Our work is a first step toward the realization of a cavity optomechanics platform with an incorporated single photon emitter.
articles.summary_en: Researchers integrated single-photon emitters in commercially available hexagonal boron nitride flakes with a hybrid silicon-nitride membrane and fiber cavity. The platform simultaneously demonstrates membrane vibrational modes and cavity-coupled emission, supporting future cavity optomechanics and quantum-photonics applications.

articles.title_original: Electrostatic Doping of Moiré Superlattices Controls the Optical Fingerprint of a WSe_2 /Twisted Bilayer Graphene heterostructure
articles.title_en: Electrostatic Doping Tunes Optical Signatures in WSe₂–Twisted Bilayer Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: We theoretically investigate the optical response of the WSe2 monolayer vertically stacked on twisted bilayer graphene (tBG) under electrostatic doping. In this heterostructure, the doped moiré superlattice of tBG generates a spatially modulated electrostatic potential that couples to the electron and hole constituents of the WSe2 exciton through the screened Coulomb interaction, thereby providing a microscopic mechanism for exciton coupling to the charge-density landscape of the moiré Fermi sea. Focusing on twist angles below the magic angle (1.1°), where electronic correlations are strongly enhanced, we demonstrate that electrostatic doping induces pronounced modifications of the excitonic absorption spectrum, including the emergence of multiple satellite resonances. We show that these spectral features originate from the interplay between the exciton center-of-mass and internal degrees of freedom, together with doping-induced hybridization between Rydberg exciton states of different orbital symmetry. The calculated spectra are in good agreement with previously reported experimental observations and theoretical predictions. Our results establish electrostatic doping in tBG as an effective means of engineering excitonic states in adjacent semiconducting monolayers and provide a pathway toward novel optical sensor devices.
articles.summary_en: Theoretical research shows that electrostatic doping of twisted bilayer graphene modifies excitonic absorption in adjacent WSe₂, producing satellite resonances through moiré-driven interactions and exciton-state hybridization. The findings support tunable excitonic devices and potential optical sensor applications.

articles.title_original: Defect‐Mediated Inelastic Light Scattering by Infrared Phonons in Hexagonal Boron Nitride
articles.title_en: Defect-engineered hBN enables infrared-phonon light scattering
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Phonons in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) possess exceptionally strong oscillator strengths, giving rise to hyperbolic phonon polaritons and enabling robust phonon‐mediated nonlinear interactions. Defect states in hBN are known to interact strongly with lattice vibrations, yet the role of defects in enabling inelastic optical scattering through otherwise Raman‐inactive, infrared (IR)‐active phonon modes remains largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate a highly efficient inelastic phonon scattering mechanism in which the general selection rules are violated, leading to a down‐converted laser emission mediated by IR‐active phonons in defect‐engineered hBN, via stimulated Raman scattering. We further show that the phonon landscape of hBN can be tailored through substrate choice, enabling multiple inelastic scattering processes and sequential down‐conversion of the excitation laser frequency. These results establish a general strategy for nonlinear defect–phonon scattering and tailoring the nonlinear‐optical selection rules in hBN.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate defect-mediated stimulated Raman scattering in hexagonal boron nitride, enabling laser down-conversion through normally inactive infrared phonons. Substrate engineering further enables sequential frequency conversion, suggesting opportunities for nonlinear photonics and optoelectronic devices.

articles.title_original: Effect of Graphene Oxide and Surface-Functionalized Graphene Oxide on the Mechanical Performance of EPDM/NBR Composites
articles.title_en: Silane-Functionalized Graphene Oxide Strengthens EPDM/NBR Composites
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract EPDM/NBR elastomer blends reinforced with silane-treated graphene oxide were successfully fabricated to enhance their overall performance. Graphene oxide (GO) was synthesized using a modified Hummers oxidation route and subsequently chemically functionalized with γ-aminopropyltriethoxysilane (KH550) to strengthen its compatibility with the rubber matrix. This chemical modification significantly improved the distribution of the nanofiller within the elastomeric system relative to unmodified graphene oxide, resulting in more effective stress transfer between the filler and polymer phases. As a result, the composites containing functionalized graphene oxide demonstrated notable improvements in mechanical behavior. At an optimized filler concentration of 5 phr, the tensile strength, stress at 100% elongation, and tear resistance increased by 36.2, 19.4, and 57.1%, respectively. Furthermore, these reinforced materials exhibited superior resistance to abrasive wear compared with both unfilled blends and those containing untreated graphene oxide. The enhanced performance is primarily associated with uniform nanofiller dispersion and stronger interfacial interactions established through silane functionalization. Overall, the incorporation of KH550-modified graphene oxide (KH550-GO) represents a promising and practical approach for producing advanced elastomeric materials with improved durability and mechanical integrity for demanding engineering applications such as automotive components and sealing technologies.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report that KH550-functionalized graphene oxide improved filler dispersion and interfacial bonding in EPDM/NBR elastomer blends. At 5 phr, tensile strength, stress at 100% elongation, and tear resistance increased by 36.2%, 19.4%, and 57.1%, respectively, alongside improved abrasive-wear resistance.

articles.title_original: Excitation-Energy-Dependent Enhancement of Hot-Carrier Lifetimes in Graphene
articles.title_en: Graphene Hot-Carrier Lifetimes Strongly Depend on Excitation Energy
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Understanding hot-carrier relaxation in graphene is important for ultrafast optoelectronic and terahertz technologies. Here, we investigate carrier cooling dynamics in mono- and bilayer graphene using mid-infrared pump pulses (0.22 to 0.73 eV) and terahertz probe pulses. We uncover a pronounced, reproducible, and nonmonotonic dependence of the carrier relaxation time on excitation photon energy. Within a narrow spectral window from 0.42 to 0.48 eV, the carrier lifetime increases by nearly an order of magnitude compared to the few-picosecond cooling observed at lower and higher excitation energies. The observed excitation-energy dependence is consistent with a hot-phonon bottleneck scenario in which the accumulation and reabsorption of nonequilibrium optical phonons suppress the energy transfer to the lattice. A phenomenological coupled carrier–phonon model supports this interpretation. These findings reveal a previously unreported excitation-energy dependence of hot-carrier cooling in graphene and provide new insight into nonequilibrium carrier–phonon interactions near the optical-phonon bottleneck.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report a pronounced, nonmonotonic dependence of hot-carrier relaxation time on excitation photon energy in mono- and bilayer graphene. A narrow 0.42–0.48 eV window extends carrier lifetimes by nearly an order of magnitude, consistent with a hot-phonon bottleneck and relevant to ultrafast optoelectronic and terahertz technologies.

articles.title_original: 3D printed polymer graphene nanocomposites for bio-sensor applications
articles.title_en: 3D-Printed Graphene Polymer Composites Enable Prosthetic Strain Sensors
articles.excerpt_original: Prosthetic technology lacks effective, 3D-printable strain sensors for enhancing sensory feedback. This study explores the potential of thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) and polyamide 11 (PA11) blends with graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs) to address this challenge. The composites were extruded using a twin-screw extruder. Raman spectroscopy and atomic force microscopy (AFM) were used to analyse GNPs. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) were conducted on neat polymers and composites to characterise the sample thermally. Structural analysis was done via X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), Raman mapping and oscillating rheology. Tensile testing was carried out on filaments and 3D-printed dumbbells according to relevant ISO standards 2062 and 527, respectively. Electrical testing was done on all the samples, and electro-mechanical testing was done on all samples in which the resistance could be detected on a standard multimeter. In TPU, 1.5 wt. % GNP loading optimised phase separation and order; however, more importantly, the ductility properties of the TPU were not affected by the presence of GNPs. In PA11, an electrical percolation threshold was achieved at 7.9 wt% GNPs, yielding a gauge factor of 13.25 ± 3.31 at 10 wt. %. The TPU/PA11 blend maintained TPU's ductility while incorporating PA11's electrical properties. Single-material FDM printing of TPU//PA11/10GNP blend achieved a gauge factor of 1.63 ± 0.08, outperforming dual-material prints. This study demonstrates the feasibility of creating a 3D-printable TPU/PA11/GNP composite material with strain-sensing capabilities, potentially advancing the development of more responsive prosthetic devices. Thesis embargoed until 31 July 2030.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed 3D-printable TPU/PA11 composites containing graphene nanoplatelets for prosthetic strain sensing. A single-material TPU/PA11/10GNP blend achieved a gauge factor of 1.63 ± 0.08 while retaining TPU’s ductility, demonstrating potential for responsive prosthetic devices.

articles.title_original: Application of Nanocellulose/Graphene Oxide Composites in Supercapacitors
articles.title_en: Nanocellulose–Graphene Oxide Composite Improves Supercapacitor Performance
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Graphene is an ideal electrode material for supercapacitors, yet its electrochemical performance is severely impaired by interlayer stacking and aggregation. To address this issue, nanocellulose (NC) extracted from corn stalks was used as a spacer to construct nanocellulose/graphene oxide (GO) composites, thus inhibiting the restacking of graphene sheets. A one-step hydrothermal method was adopted for the composite preparation: NC derived from pretreated corn stalks was mixed with GO solution, and the hydrothermal reactions were conducted at 180 °Ｃ, 200 °Ｃ and 220 °Ｃ, respectively. The as-prepared composites were characterized by SEM, TEM, XRD, XPS, Raman spectroscopy and nitrogen adsorption-desorption measurements, and their electrochemical performances were systematically investigated. The results show that hydrothermal temperature exerts a decisive effect on the microstructural properties of the composites, with the sample prepared at 200 °C exhibiting good comprehensive performance within the tested range. Characterization results confirm the formation of a continuous porous 3D network structure in the composite, where NC effectively hinders the interlayer stacking of GO. Electrochemical tests demonstrate that the GO-NC-200 composite possesses good specific capacitance and excellent charge transfer capability, delivering an areal capacitance of 6.80 F/cm2 and a gravimetric capacitance of 311.74 F/g at a current density of 0.1 A/cm2.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a porous three-dimensional nanocellulose/graphene oxide composite using corn-stalk-derived nanocellulose as a spacer to limit graphene-sheet restacking. The sample prepared at 200°C achieved an areal capacitance of 6.80 F/cm² and gravimetric capacitance of 311.74 F/g, indicating potential for supercapacitor electrodes.

articles.title_original: A protective oxide strategy for stable graphene gas sensors
articles.title_en: Protective oxide stabilizes graphene gas sensors
articles.excerpt_original: Graphene is an exceptional transducer for chemical sensing owing to its two-dimensional structure and distinctive electronic properties. However, coupling graphene to noble-metal catalysts remains intrinsically challenging: catalytic oxygen dissociation, essential for sensing many gases and volatile analytes, produces reactive oxygen species that irreversibly oxidize graphene and degrade device performance. Here we overcome this limitation with a heterostructure architecture that spatially decouples catalytic activation from the graphene conduction channel, demonstrated for CO sensing. An ultrathin Sb₂O₃ interlayer inserted between CVD graphene and a platinum catalyst serves as a chemically inert barrier that suppresses oxidative attack while maintaining charge-transfer-based transduction. The resulting Pt/Sb₂O₃/graphene devices deliver reproducible CO sensing during prolonged heating, in ozone-rich atmospheres and after 20 months of ambient storage. This architecture provides a general route to stable catalyst-integrated graphene gas sensors.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a Pt/Sb₂O₃/graphene heterostructure that separates catalytic oxygen activation from the graphene sensing channel, reducing oxidative degradation during CO detection. The devices maintained reproducible performance under prolonged heating, ozone exposure, and 20 months of ambient storage.

articles.title_original: Design and optimization of surface plasmon resonance methane sensor based on graphene-silver layer
articles.title_en: Graphene–Silver SPR Sensor Enables Selective Methane Detection
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Methane is a flammable and explosive gas; therefore, its rapid and high-selectivity detection is crucial for workplace safety and environmental protection. Nevertheless, current sensing technologies still struggle to simultaneously achieve high sensitivity and long-term stability. To address this issue, this paper proposes a high-sensitivity methane gas sensor based on the Kretschmann configuration, which adopts a composite structure consisting of a BK7 prism, silver film, graphene, and Cryptophane-A. After structural parameter optimization, the sensor delivers an excellent sensing response for methane with a volume fraction ranging from 1.5% to 3.0%, and its volume fraction sensitivity reaches 0.79°/%. The proposed sensor effectively overcomes the stability drawbacks of conventional detection methods, providing a feasible solution for rapid, high-selectivity and on-line monitoring of methane gas.
articles.summary_en: Researchers designed and optimized a surface plasmon resonance methane sensor using a silver film, graphene, and Cryptophane-A. The sensor achieved a reported volume-fraction sensitivity of 0.79°/% across 1.5%–3.0% methane, supporting rapid online monitoring.

articles.title_original: MXene for Brain-Computer Interfaces: A Critical Mini-Review
articles.title_en: Review Highlights MXene Potential for Brain–Computer Interfaces
articles.excerpt_original: Brain-computer interfaces have attracted extensive attention for applications in neuroprosthetics, rehabilitation, and human-machine interaction in recent years. One key challenge in brain-computer interface development is the construction of neural interfaces capable of stable and efficient communication between neural tissues and electronic devices. Recently, MXenes, two-dimensional layered transition metal carbides and nitrides, have emerged as promising materials for brain-computer interface applications owing to their unique structures and physicochemical properties, e.g. , metallic conductivity, high mechanical strength, flexible processability, and tunable surface chemistry and biocompatibility. To clarify why MXenes are inherently suitable for brain-computer interface devices, this work reviews their synthesis, electrical characteristics, mechanical flexibility, and biocompatibility, which collectively address critical neural device requirements such as charge injection at the bio-interface and long-term compatibility. We then survey demonstrated applications of MXene-based devices in neural recording, stimulation, and multimodal functions. Finally, we discuss the remaining challenges and prospects for MXene-based brain-computer interfaces, followed by a brief comparison discussion of other two-dimensional materials such as graphene, molybdenum disulfide, two-dimensional organic frameworks. This work contributes to the future development of two-dimensional materials-enabled brain-computer devices by bridging materials science and neural engineering.
articles.summary_en: A critical mini-review examines MXenes for neural recording, stimulation, and multimodal brain–computer interfaces. It assesses their conductivity, flexibility, surface chemistry, and biocompatibility while identifying remaining development challenges and comparing them with graphene and other two-dimensional materials.

articles.title_original: Rapid Synthesis of Ti3C2Tx MXene for Memristor Applications
articles.title_en: Rapid Low-Temperature Synthesis of Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene for Memristors
articles.excerpt_original: Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene was synthesised via an optimised low-temperature molten salt method using ammonium bifluoride. Complete MAX (Ti3AlC2) phase etching was achieved within 5 minutes at a temperature of 150 °C. Structural and compositional characterisation of Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene confirmed well-exfoliated Ti3C2Tx sheets with com-plete Al removal. The synthesised Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene was integrated as the active switch-ing layer in lateral and vertical memristor geometries. Both geometries exhibited non-linear bipolar resistive switching. The vertical device exhibited an on-state current of ~10 mA and stable resistance retention of over 120 minutes. UV-Ozone treatment of lateral devices resulted in the I-V characteristics changing from bipolar to asymmetric with rectifying characteristics. These results establish a broadly accessible, low-cost prototyping framework for Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene -based memristor devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a low-temperature molten-salt method that etches Ti₃AlC₂ to produce well-exfoliated Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene in five minutes at 150 °C. The material enabled non-linear bipolar resistive switching in lateral and vertical memristors, with the vertical device retaining stable resistance for over 120 minutes.

articles.title_original: Mxene@PEG Hybrid Molecularly Imprinted Electrochemical Interface for Ultrasensitive Detection of Mucin-1
articles.title_en: MXene–PEG molecularly imprinted sensor detects breast cancer biomarker Mucin-1
articles.excerpt_original: Breast cancer is among the most prevalent cancers in women and poses significant global health challenges. In various types of cancer, such as those affecting especially the breast, pancreas, and lung, the cells that constitute the tumor tissues have been observed to produce a transmembrane glycoprotein known as Mucin-1 (MUC-1). This study presents an electrochemical sensor with great selectivity and sensitivity for MUC-1 detection, characterized by the exceptional properties of a hybrid system comprising MXene and molecularly imprinted polymer (MIP). The surface of a screen printed carbon electrode (SPCE) was modified using a solution of MXene and polyethylene glycol (PEG), followed by the formation of a MIP layer through electrochemical polymerization utilizing pyrrole as the functional monomer. Under optimal settings, the MIP-based nanosensor MUC-1 exhibited a linear response within the concentration range of 5–100 fg/mL. The performance of the assay was characterized by a sensitivity of 0.17 fg/mL, as demonstrated in standard solutions. The LOD of the assay was established at 1.47 fg/mL when applied to commercial serum samples, thereby providing quantitative sensitivity to detect low-abundance analytes. The selectivity of the sensor was analyzed in the presence of diverse interfering agents, and the computations of the selectivity coefficient (k) were conducted using biomarkers with analogous protein structures. Consequently, upon examination of additional validation parameters, the findings demonstrated high reproducibility, excellent selectivity, and stability. This study demonstrates the potential for MUC-1 detection in clinical and point-of-care settings, and also provides as a framework for the identification of other biomarkers.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed an electrochemical nanosensor combining MXene, polyethylene glycol and a molecularly imprinted polymer for ultrasensitive Mucin-1 detection. The device achieved a reported detection limit of 1.47 fg/mL in serum, indicating potential for clinical and point-of-care biomarker testing.

articles.title_en: Magnetically Engineered MXenes Advance Water Remediation and Oil Separation

Despite the rapidly growing number of studies on MMXenes, a comprehensive understanding of the structure-property-performance relationships governing their hazardous metal-ion adsorption and oil-separation behavior, as well as their use in the valorization of used cooking oil (UCO), remains limited. This review critically examines recent advances in the design, characterization, and environmental applications of MMXene-based composites for heavy-metal treatment, oil-water separation, and UCO conversion to fuels. articles.summary_en: This review examines ferrite-integrated MXenes for heavy-metal adsorption, oil–water separation, and conversion of used cooking oil into biodiesel.
