articles.title_original: MXenes for Boosting Potassium Ion Storage: Structure‐Property Relationships, Interface Science, Microscopic Mechanisms, and Application Perspectives
articles.title_en: Review Examines MXenes for Potassium-Ion Battery Anodes
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Potassium‐ion batteries (PIBs) have attracted significant attention owing to the abundance and low cost of potassium resources. However, their practical development remains hindered by anode‐related challenges, including sluggish kinetics and pronounced volume variation during cycling. MXenes provide a promising platform for addressing these issues because of their two‐dimensional layered architecture, high electrical conductivity, and tunable surface chemistry. This Review provides a critical overview of recent advances in MXene‐based anodes for PIBs, with emphasis on interlayer spacing expansion, surface termination regulation, and heterostructure design. It also examines the underlying potassium‐storage mechanisms, including intercalation, pseudocapacitive storage, conversion reactions, and alloying‐related processes. The discussion examines how interfacial charge transfer, defect engineering, and the “trapping‐conversion” mechanism contribute to improved electrochemical performance. Finally, this review discusses key challenges associated with MXene‐based PIB anodes, including interfacial instability, full‐cell compatibility, and performance verification under practical operating conditions. Future perspectives are proposed for advancing MXene‐based potassium storage materials through multidimensional structural regulation, interfacial engineering, and mechanism‐guided material design.
articles.summary_en: This review assesses how MXene structure, surface chemistry, interlayer spacing, and heterostructure design can improve potassium storage. It identifies interfacial instability, full-cell compatibility, and practical performance validation as key barriers to commercialization.

articles.title_original: Preparation and Thermal Properties of Myristic Acid/Hydrophobic Fumed Silica/Hexagonal Boron Nitride Composite Phase Change Material
articles.title_en: Boron Nitride Composite Improves Phase-Change Thermal Storage Performance
articles.excerpt_original: To address the issues of leakage and poor thermal conductivity in organic solid-liquid phase change materials, this study prepared a shape-stabilized composite phase change material using myristic acid (MA) as the phase change energy storage matrix, hydrophobic fumed silica (FS) as the porous carrier, and hexagonal boron nitride (BN) as the thermally conductive filler via a solvent-assisted impregnation method. The composite material was characterized by scanning electron microscopy, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, and differential scanning calorimetry. The results indicate that the composite with an MA mass fraction of 65 % exhibits both satisfactory shape stability and a relatively high latent heat of phase change. The sample with 2 % BN addition demonstrates the best overall performance, with melting and solidification temperatures of 52.47 °C and 51.89 °C, and melting and solidification latent heats of 115.6 J/g and 110.8 J/g, respectively. The thermal conductivity is increased by 83.6% compared to the composite without BN, and the addition of BN also showed a preliminary effect in reducing the supercooling degree. The composite system shows application potential for low‑to‑medium temperature solar thermal storage, providing a theoretical basis and technical reference for the development of efficient, low‑cost, and scalable phase change energy storage materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a myristic acid, hydrophobic fumed silica and hexagonal boron nitride composite phase-change material for low- to medium-temperature solar thermal storage. A 2% boron nitride addition increased thermal conductivity by 83.6% while maintaining latent heat of up to 115.6 J/g.

articles.title_original: Low-Temperature Synthesis of Large-Area Hexagonal Boron Nitride Films on Diverse Substrates by Plasma Afterglow Deposition
articles.title_en: Low-Temperature Plasma Growth Enables Large-Area hBN Films on Diverse Substrates
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is a van der Waals material with excellent insulating properties that make it well-suited as a gate dielectric in 2D electronic devices. In recent years, the discovery of an ever-increasing list of properties has led to a much broader range of potential applications, including quantum photonics, memristive devices, and extreme-environment coatings. However, current growth methods for hBN films are characterized by a narrow selection of substrates and high temperatures that require transfer and limit scale-up. Here, we report a remote plasma-activated approach to directly synthesize large-area hBN films on a diverse range of representative metallic, semiconducting, and amorphous insulating substrates. Specifically, we employ the spatial afterglow of an Ar/H2 plasma to activate ammonia borane, which enables the growth of thick (>30 nm), uniform, and stoichiometric films on substrates such as Si, SiO2, glass, fused silica, Mo, and Al. Systematic spectroscopic characterization reveals that hBN films can be grown as low as 300 °C. Furthermore, plasma afterglow-grown hBN films exhibit mechanical, electrical, and thermal properties on par with or exceeding those reported by alternate synthesis methods. These results establish plasma afterglow growth for the direct integration of hBN into a wide range of emerging technologies.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate direct synthesis of uniform, stoichiometric hexagonal boron nitride films on metallic, semiconducting, and insulating substrates at temperatures as low as 300 °C. The approach could support scalable integration of hBN as a gate dielectric and in other emerging electronic and extreme-environment applications.

articles.title_original: RF Power Independence of the Optical Band Gap in Boron Nitride Thin Films on Silicon
articles.title_en: RF Power Has Little Effect on BN Thin-Film Optical Band Gap
articles.excerpt_original: Boron nitride (BN) thin films have attracted considerable interest because of their excellent thermal stability, high dielectric breakdown strength, and wide optical band gap, making them attractive for advanced optoelectronic and insulating applications. Among the available deposition techniques, RF magnetron sputtering is advantageous because it enables controlled film growth at relatively low temperatures. Although many studies have reported BN thin-film deposition, the specific influence of RF power on the optical properties of room-temperature deposited films remains poorly understood. Clarifying this effect is important for optimizing deposition conditions and obtaining high-quality BN coatings. This study examines how RF power affects the optical properties and band structure of BN thin films deposited at room temperature. The films were deposited on double-sided polished, (100)-oriented silicon wafers using a 99.5% pure hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) target in an argon atmosphere (~0.3 Pa) for 30 minutes, with RF power varied between 100 and 190 W. Optical characterization was performed using UV–visible spectroscopy (200–800 nm). We calculated the absorption coefficient from the absorbance spectra and estimated the optical band gap using Tauc plots ((αhν)² vs. hν). Data processing and curve fitting were conducted using Python and UVProbe. The band gap ranged from 6.03 to 6.09 eV, showing negligible variation with RF power, indicating stable stoichiometry and bonding. These findings show that room-temperature sputtering produces BN thin films with consistent optical properties suitable for wide-band-gap optoelectronic and dielectric applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers found that boron nitride thin films deposited by room-temperature RF magnetron sputtering maintained a stable optical band gap of 6.03–6.09 eV across 100–190 W. The results support use of these films in wide-band-gap optoelectronic and dielectric applications.

articles.title_original: Low contact resistance and high current density in ballistic p-type transistors based on oxygen-doped WSe2 monolayers
articles.title_en: Oxygen-Doped WSe2 Enables High-Current Ballistic p-Type Transistors
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The development of high-performance p-type monolayer transistors is critical for extending two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors beyond silicon in sub 1-nm technology nodes for complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) circuits. However, insufficient doping and metal-induced gap states (MIGS) during metal deposition lead to high contact resistance, greatly limiting p-type on-state currents. Here, we demonstrate high-performance ballistic p-type monolayer tungsten diselenide (WSe 2 ) transistors by oxygen p-doping. The controllable oxygen doping greatly reduces the number of Se vacancy defects in as-grown WSe 2 , and thus increases the hole mobility from 55 to 218.3 cm 2 V −1 s −1 —approaching the theoretical limit. Moreover, this approach also induces a heavily hole-doped contact region in p-type monolayer WSe 2 devices and decreases the contact resistance from 1869 Ω·μm down to 104 Ω·μm. Consequently, a 16-nm-channel WSe 2 p-type field effect transistor (pFET) delivers a saturation current of up to 1635 μA μm −1 at a drain voltage of −1.2 V and a ballistic ratio as high as 81% at room temperature.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated oxygen-doped monolayer WSe2 p-type transistors with improved hole mobility and sharply reduced contact resistance. A 16-nm-channel device achieved 1,635 μA μm−1 saturation current and an 81% room-temperature ballistic ratio, supporting 2D semiconductor applications below the 1-nm technology-node era.

articles.title_original: Synthesis of a 2D/2D g-C3N4/UiO-66 S-scheme heterojunction for enhanced photocatalytic degradation of organic pollutants
articles.title_en: 2D g-C3N4/UiO-66 Heterojunction Improves Photocatalytic Wastewater Treatment
articles.excerpt_original: A unique 2D/2D g-C 3 N 4 /UiO-66 S-scheme nano-heterojunction was successfully developed via a straightforward hydrothermal approach to enhance the photocatalytic decomposition of organic contaminants under visible light. Comprehensive characterization techniques were employed to systematically examine the properties of the individual semiconductors and the newly synthesized heterostructure. PL, EIS and PR analyses confirmed that the photo-generated charge carries in 2D/2D nano-heterojunction/visible-light system have been efficiently separated. The improved photocatalytic performance could be ascribed to the strong contact between nanosheets of two semiconductors, uniform dispersion of UiO-66 nanosheets on the surface of large g-C 3 N 4 nanosheets and synergistic effect of S-scheme electron-hole migration. The nano-heterojunction synthesized at the mass ratio of 0.2:1 of UiO-66 nanosheets to g-C 3 N 4 nanosheets, g-C 3 N 4 /UiO-66/20, exhibited the highest MB photo-degradation rate (70.19% and 98.25% at catalyst dosages of 0.1 and 0.3 g/L, respectively), where the kinetic constant is 2.53 and 4.10 times of pristine g-C 3 N 4 and UiO-66, respectively. Quenching experiments identified \(\:{.O}_{2}^{-}\) , \(\:.OH\) and \(\:{h}^{+}\) as the predominant active species, in descending order of importance. g-C 3 N 4 /UiO-66/20 nano-heterojunction indicated tremendous reusability and consistency, and it can be employed to successively uptake pollutant molecules from wastewater. This paper paves the way to construction of new visible-light driven 2D/2D nano-heterojunctions for the wastewater treatment process.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a 2D/2D g-C3N4/UiO-66 S-scheme heterojunction that enhances visible-light degradation of organic pollutants. The optimized catalyst achieved up to 98.25% methylene blue degradation and showed reusability in wastewater treatment tests.

articles.title_original: Giant Anisotropic Spin Absorption in Chiral Hybrid Semiconductors
articles.title_en: Chiral Hybrid Semiconductors Enable Strongly Anisotropic Spin Absorption
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Control of spin‐current absorption in non‐magnetic materials is central to realizing spin‐current switches and low‐power spintronic technologies, yet anisotropic responses have so far been limited to a narrow class of crystalline materials. Here we demonstrate giant chirality‐induced anisotropic spin‐current absorption (CASA) in solution‐processed chiral hybrid organic–inorganic semiconductors (HOISs), establishing them as a versatile platform for symmetry‐selective spin manipulation. Zero‐dimensional [ R/S/rac ‐MBA] 4 Bi 2 Cl 10 (MBA = α ‐methylbenzylammonium) HOISs exhibit more than an order‐of‐magnitude variation in spin absorption between orthogonal spin polarizations. Strikingly, despite the lack of chiroptical activity, racemic films exhibit a similarly strong spin anisotropy, indicating that global crystallographic chirality is not a prerequisite for CASA. Structural chirality analysis reveals that the CASA is governed by the orientation of local chiral axes associated with the organic cations in HOISs. These results establish molecular chirality as an active design parameter for manipulating spin transport, positioning HOISs as a broadly compelling platform for spin‐based functionalities.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated more than an order-of-magnitude variation in spin-current absorption across orthogonal polarizations in solution-processed chiral hybrid organic–inorganic semiconductors. The findings identify local molecular chirality as a design parameter for spin transport and potential spintronic devices.

articles.source: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
articles.title_original: Adsorptive Removal of F⁻ and P2O5 From Real Phosphogypsum Leachate Using Graphene Oxide and Reduced Graphene Oxide: Performance Evaluation and Process Parameter Optimization
articles.title_en: Graphene Oxide Adsorbents Remove Fluoride and Phosphorus from Phosphogypsum Leachate
articles.summary_en: Academic research evaluates graphene oxide and reduced graphene oxide for adsorptive removal of fluoride and P2O5 from real phosphogypsum leachate. The study optimizes process parameters and assesses treatment performance for challenging industrial wastewater.

articles.title_original: Accessing multi-band transport in bilayer graphene charge-transfer interfaces
articles.title_en: Bilayer graphene interfaces enable gate-controlled multiband transport
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Placing atomically thin carbon layers in close proximity with other van der Waals materials can result in a wide range of emergent phenomena driven by multiple proximity effects, which can modify their low-energy band structure and/or shift the Fermi level away from charge neutrality. Here we show that charge transfer at bilayer graphene (BLG)/MnPS 3 interfaces is sufficiently large to populate the higher-lying (HLy) energy valence band of BLG, enabling the investigation of multi-band transport, which can be turned ON and OFF using a conventional gate. The onset of multi-band transport results in the appearance of a dozen Shubnikov-de Haas (SdH) oscillation frequencies, whose origin can be traced to mixing of the two fundamental frequencies that map the Fermi contour of the HLy- and lower-lying (LLy) valence bands of BLG, and a third frequency whose origin is yet to be identified. Multi-band transport also results in the emergence of a non-linear Hall effect, whose analysis in terms of a classical two-carrier model enables the determination of the carrier density and mobility in both bands. We find that the onset of multi-band transport takes place at a hole density ≈2.9 × 10 13 cm −2 , in good agreement with the value extracted from the SdH frequencies. In turn, the mobility is found to be 10 000 and 4000 cm 2 Vs −1 for holes in the HLy- and LLy-energy bands, respectively. The possibility to reach the high carrier densities needed to access multiband transport, while retaining the sufficiently high mobility needed to detect SdH oscillations, demonstrates that charge transfer interfaces provide a non-destructive route to investigate transport phenomena not accessible via conventional gates.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate that charge transfer at bilayer graphene–MnPS₃ interfaces populates a higher-energy valence band, enabling gate-controlled multiband transport. The platform retains sufficient mobility to reveal Shubnikov–de Haas oscillations and nonlinear Hall effects, offering access to transport regimes unavailable with conventional gating.

articles.title_original: Two-dimensional gate dielectrics for field-effect transistors: from h-BN to emerging vdW and quasi-vdW materials
articles.title_en: Review Surveys 2D Gate Dielectrics for Beyond-Silicon Transistors
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Recent progress in two-dimensional (2D) materials has generated immense interest in their use in field-effect transistors (FETs) for beyond-silicon electronics. Among them, 2D van der Waals (vdW) dielectrics play a pivotal role in facilitating high-performance, low-power devices, as they offer atomically smooth surfaces, no dangling bonds, and high electrostatic control. This review focuses on the latest developments in 2D vdW and quasi-vdW dielectrics, with emphasis on their electrical properties optimized for FETs. We highlighted the integration challenges of 3D dielectric materials for 2D semiconductors. Starting from hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) and newly discovered dielectric materials such as rare-earth oxyhalides, transition metal oxyhalides, rare-earth oxysulfide, native oxide, muscovite mica, ferroelectric, alkaline-earth hydroxides, transition-metal nitride halides, quasi 2D dielectrics, and perovskite-based dielectrics are thoroughly discussed by highlighting their transistor performance. Device integration with these dielectrics has also been discussed. Finally, we discussed perspectives for future work to improve the 2D dielectric properties and scalability and realize compatibility with complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) technology.
articles.summary_en: The review examines h-BN and emerging van der Waals and quasi-van der Waals dielectrics for field-effect transistors, emphasizing electrical performance and device integration. It identifies scalability and CMOS compatibility as key remaining challenges for practical adoption.

articles.title_original: Fluctuation-induced magnetoresistance in graphene Hall bars at charge neutrality
articles.title_en: Theory Explains Fluctuation-Induced Magnetoresistance in Graphene Hall Bars
articles.excerpt_original: In the temperature interval $T\sim 50 - 100 K$, the rate of electron-electron collisions in graphene devices may exceed the momentum relaxation rate due to disorder and electron-phonon scattering. In this regime, the motion of the electron liquid may be described by the hydrodynamic equations. In the hydrodynamic approximation, at the charge neutrality point the electric current is decoupled from the hydrodynamic flow, and the conductivity of the system is equal to the intrinsic conductivity of the electron liquid, $σ_0$. It was recently shown that the coupling of charge transport and hydrodynamic flow induced by the thermal fluctuations enhances the macroscopic conductivity of the system and results in very strong positive magnetoresistance (MR) at relatively weak fields. Here we develop a quantitative theory of the fluctuation mechanism of MR at charge neutrality and obtain analytic expressions for MR in graphene Hall bars. The functional dependence of MR on the magnetic field $H$ is sensitive to the Hall bar geometry and orientation relative to the current. We also account for the effect of momentum relaxation on MR.
articles.summary_en: Researchers develop a quantitative theory for strong positive magnetoresistance in charge-neutral graphene under hydrodynamic conditions. The model shows that magnetic-field response depends on Hall-bar geometry, orientation, and momentum relaxation, with potential relevance to graphene magnetotransport and sensing research.

articles.title_original: Weak non-Landau-type contributions to the diamagnetism of graphite
articles.title_en: Study Quantifies Non-Landau Diamagnetic Contributions in Graphite
articles.excerpt_original: The exceptionally large diamagnetic susceptibility of a single-crystal graphite in the direction perpendicular to the graphene layers is caused by the Landau levels. However, there are also other contributions to the magnetic susceptibility. In particular, in metals the Pauli paramagnetism is leading, whereas in dielectrics the diamagnetic Langevin and paramagnetic Van Vleck terms are essential. These components of magnetic susceptibility are also present in graphite. In this work, we calculate the magnitudes of all these small contributions from first principles. It is found that the Pauli paramagnetism is negligible (2.3 x 10^{-9} emu/g), whereas the other diamagnetic contribution - arising from the Langevin and Van Vleck mechanisms - is comparable to the in-plane experimental diamagnetism of graphite and to the diamagnetic response of C60 and C70} fullerenes. This diamagnetic contribution proves to be slightly anisotropic (-2.93 x 10^{-7} emu/g along the x- or y-axes and -2.24 x 10^{-7} emu/g along the $z-$axis), with the averaged value -2.7 x 10^{-7} emu/g.
articles.summary_en: First-principles calculations show that Pauli paramagnetism is negligible in graphite, while Langevin and Van Vleck diamagnetism is comparable to graphite’s in-plane response. The non-Landau contribution is slightly anisotropic and averages −2.7 × 10⁻⁷ emu/g.

articles.title_original: Ultrathin-Gap MXene/Carbon Nanotube Microsupercapacitors for High-Performance Alternating Current-Line Filtering
articles.title_en: MXene/CNT Microsupercapacitors Enable High-Performance AC-Line Filtering
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The continued miniaturization of modern electronic devices has created an urgent demand for next-generation AC-line filtering capacitors capable of replacing conventional aluminum electrolytic capacitors. Here, we report a high-performance AC-line filter based on MXene/CNT liquid crystal, fabricated into cross-finger electrodes via spin coating followed by supercritical drying. Precise control over the interelectrode gap width was achieved using femtosecond laser direct writing, enabling gap sizes as small as 5 µm. Systematic electrochemical characterization reveals that the electrode with a 5 µm gap width exhibits an ultralow equivalent series resistance of 0.15 Ω cm2 and a highly negative phase angle of –84° at 120 Hz. Owing to rapid ion transport within MXene/CNT architecture and the ultranarrow electrode spacing, the device delivers superior high-frequency response with a 0.1 ms relaxation time constant, and efficient AC-line filtering performance. These results demonstrate the strong potential of MXene-based microsupercapacitors as compact, high-performance alternatives to traditional electrolytic capacitors for powering next-generation electronic systems.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed MXene/carbon nanotube microsupercapacitors with 5 µm electrode gaps, achieving low resistance, rapid relaxation, and effective 120 Hz AC-line filtering. The work suggests a compact alternative to aluminum electrolytic capacitors for miniaturized electronic systems, although commercial readiness is not established.

articles.title_original: Unlocking the catalytic potential of finite nanoporous hBN-C[3]A: A single-atom strategy for sustainable water splitting
articles.title_en: hBN-C[3]A Framework Shows Promise for Single-Atom Water-Splitting Catalysts
articles.excerpt_original: The development of efficient electrocatalysts for water splitting is essential for sustainable hydrogen production. We present a density functional theory investigation of a novel cyclic anthracene-based hexagonal boron nitride framework (hBN-C[3]A) as a platform for single-atom catalysts. We systematically evaluate the structural stability, electronic properties, and catalytic performance of pristine hBN-C[3]A and its Fe, Ni, Mo, and Ru-decorated derivatives. All metal-decorated configurations exhibit negative binding energies (−0.33 to −0.52 eV) and positive vibrational frequencies, confirming stability. Electronic analysis reveals that metal decoration introduces states near the Fermi level, reducing the energy gap from 4.64 eV to as low as 0.83 eV. Remarkably, Mo, Ni, and Ru-decorated frameworks exhibit near-thermoneutral hydrogen adsorption free energies (0.029, −0.056, and −0.096 eV), rivaling platinum for hydrogen evolution. In contrast, the pristine framework and Fe-decorated system demonstrate superior oxygen evolution performance with overpotentials of 0.383 V and 0.719 V. This striking activity dichotomy reveals a fundamental trade-off: metals that optimize hydrogen binding overbind oxygenated intermediates, while systems with balanced oxygen binding lack efficient hydrogen adsorption. These findings provide rational design principles for application-specific catalyst selection, establishing hBN-C[3]A as a versatile scaffold for sustainable energy conversion technologies.
articles.summary_en: A density functional theory study identifies finite nanoporous hBN-C[3]A decorated with Mo, Ni, or Ru as promising hydrogen-evolution catalysts, with near-thermoneutral hydrogen adsorption. Pristine and Fe-decorated structures show stronger oxygen-evolution performance, highlighting a trade-off between hydrogen and oxygen catalysis.

articles.title_original: Remote Moire Modulation of Decoupled Dirac Subsystems in Twisted Trilayer Graphene
articles.title_en: Remote Moiré Modulation Observed in Twisted Trilayer Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Moiré superlattices are generally assumed to act only at the interface where lattice mismatch or twist occurs. Here, we study charge transport in large-angle helical twisted trilayer graphene, where interlayer tunneling is strongly reduced. When only the top monolayer graphene is aligned with hBN, the electronic response reorganizes into a moiré-modulated monolayer and a remaining twisted bilayer graphene subsystem. Despite the absence of any explicit structural moiré in the twisted bilayer, we observe satellite-like features in its electronic response that run parallel to the primary spectrum and are locked to the density scale of the hBN/graphene moiré. These observations are consistent with a weak moiré-periodic electrostatic perturbation generated at the aligned interface and sensed by a spatially separated Dirac subsystem, even in the absence of coherent interlayer coupling.
articles.summary_en: Researchers observed moiré-like electronic features in a twisted bilayer graphene subsystem without direct structural moiré or coherent interlayer coupling. The findings indicate that electrostatic effects from a spatially separated hBN/graphene interface can modulate Dirac-electron responses, informing graphene-based electronic research.

articles.title_original: Detection defines dephasing in two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy of materials: Coherent field emission vs incoherent population observables
articles.title_en: Detection method reshapes dephasing measurements in 2D spectroscopy
articles.excerpt_original: The homogeneous spectral linewidth associated with light–matter interactions is a fundamental descriptor of the optical properties of materials, governed by the quantum dynamics of the condensed-matter system. We discuss here that the homogeneous linewidth measured by means of two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy depends not only on the intrinsic microscopic dynamics of the material, but also on the observable through which those dynamics are projected onto the measurement. In this Perspective, we develop a unified framework showing that identical microscopic dynamics can yield different experimentally inferred dephasing times because different detection operators project different sectors of the nonequilibrium dynamics. For coherent emitted-field measurements, the observed linewidth largely retains its conventional connection to the optical coherence time T2. By contrast, in population-detected modalities such as photoluminescence, photocurrent, and other action-detected two-dimensional spectroscopies, the apparent linewidth can additionally encode excited-state population redistribution dynamics, leading naturally to an effective coherence time T2,eff. Using a coupled-mode model propagated under a common Liouvillian, we show that identical microscopic dynamics yield distinct apparent dephasing times when projected onto coherent-emission and population-derived observables. The detection observable is, therefore, not merely part of the experimental implementation but determines what dynamical information remains experimentally observable and how homogeneous linewidths should be interpreted as material descriptors.
articles.summary_en: An AIP Publishing Perspective shows that measured homogeneous linewidths and dephasing times depend on whether experiments detect coherent emission or population-derived signals. The framework indicates that population redistribution can alter apparent coherence times, affecting interpretation of optical-material descriptors.

articles.title_original: Resolving DNA Conformations and Dynamics at the Graphene Interface by Graphene Energy Transfer
articles.title_en: Graphene Energy Transfer Resolves DNA Dynamics and Enables a Molecular Nanoelevator
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The recent discovery that double-stranded DNA stands vertically on graphene has transformed graphene from a passive quenching surface into an active platform for axial single-molecule readout, opening opportunities in biosensing, molecular materials, and nanoscale devices. Here, we use graphene energy transfer with vertical nucleic acids (GETvNA) to resolve how partially single- and double-stranded DNA constructs interact with graphene at the molecular level. Single-molecule fluorescence lifetime measurements show that dsDNA adopts both vertical and parallel orientations on graphene and reveal rare 1–3 base-pair zipping and unzipping events. We further show that the ssDNA anchor length regulates dsDNA conformation by controlling the availability of graphene binding sites for exposed nucleotides, thereby modulating partial unzipping. Finally, we demonstrate programmable axial motion using DNA hybridization and strand-displacement reactions, realizing a single-molecule DNA nanoelevator with nanometer precision. These results establish GETvNA as a platform for probing molecular interfaces and engineering DNA-based nanodevices on graphene.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used graphene energy transfer and single-molecule fluorescence measurements to characterize DNA orientations, partial unzipping, and strand motion at the graphene interface. The work demonstrates programmable nanometer-scale DNA motion, supporting potential advances in graphene-based biosensing and molecular nanodevices.

articles.title_original: A Thorough Examination of Graphene-Based Materials for CO₂ Mitigation from Storage to Conversion: Review
articles.title_en: Review Examines Graphene-Based Materials for CO₂ Capture and Conversion
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT The increasing concentration of atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) intensified global efforts to develop effective carbon mitigation technologies. Carbon capture, utilization and storage (CCUS) has emerged a promising strategy through combining CO 2 capture and subsequent conversion to value-added products, thereby contributing to greenhouse-gas reduction and the circular carbon economy. Among various candidate materials, graphene and its derivatives have drawn much attention owing to their high specific surface area, excellent electrical conductivity, outstanding chemical stability and highly tunable surface chemistry. These unique features allow graphene as an excellent CO 2 adsorbent, conductive catalyst support, electron-transport medium and active component for catalytic CO 2 conversion. This review article provides a comprehensive overview of graphene-based materials for CO 2 capture and conversion, discussing the principles of adsorption, defect engineering, design of porous structures, heteroatom doping, surface functionalization, and the production of hybrid composites. The roles of graphene in electrocatalytic, photocatalytic and photoelectrochemical CO 2 reduction are critically discussed, focusing on structure–property–performance relationships and the underlying reaction mechanisms. Current challenges such as scalable synthesis, structural stability, integrated capture-conversion systems, standardized performance evaluation and techno-economic feasibility are also analyzed. Finally, future research areas are focused on accelerating the development of graphene-enable CCUS technology for practical and sustainable carbon management.
articles.summary_en: The review assesses graphene and derivatives for CO₂ adsorption, catalytic conversion, and integrated carbon-capture systems. It highlights tunable surface chemistry and conductivity while identifying scale-up, stability, performance standardization, and techno-economic feasibility as key barriers.

articles.title_original: In-situ Electrochemical Spectroscopic Ellipsometry Characterization of Polymer and MXene Films
articles.title_en: Electrochemical Ellipsometry Improves MXene Film Analysis
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract In-situ electrochemical spectroscopic ellipsometry (EC-SE) can enable real-time monitoring of optical properties and thickness changes of surfaces and thin films. This method can provide a broad range of information on the evolution of the microenvironment of an electrode during electrochemical reactions. However, to avoid modeling artifacts, accurate data analysis is critical. Here, we outline key steps in data analysis that can help prevent overfitting and misinterpretation of results. For example, determining the refractive index of the electrolyte at the air/electrolyte interface, along with measurements of the electrode’s dielectric data in dry conditions, can yield more accurate results than simultaneous fitting of all parameters for the electrolyte and electrode. We also present detailed modeling strategies tailored to fitting in-situ cyclic voltammetry (CV) data on various types of thin films, by providing two distinct examples: the thickness change of catalyst polymer films due to swelling by the electrolyte, and the simultaneous change in thickness and optical properties of Ti3C2Tx MXene films due to both reversible (electrochromic effect) and irreversible (degradation) processes. These details can help guide the informed selection of models in similar conditions by providing practical guidelines. The step-by-step approach to modeling can be more broadly adopted to enhance the accuracy and reproducibility of EC-SE experiments for interfacial studies relevant to energy conversion and storage, as well as other electrochemical reactions.
articles.summary_en: Researchers present modeling guidelines for in-situ electrochemical spectroscopic ellipsometry of polymer and Ti3C2Tx MXene films. The approach distinguishes reversible electrochromic changes from irreversible degradation, supporting more accurate studies of electrochemical interfaces relevant to energy storage and conversion.

articles.title_original: Amorphous boron nitride as a low-k dielectric for next-generation BEOL interconnects
articles.title_en: Amorphous Boron Nitride Proposed as a Robust Low-k Dielectric for BEOL Interconnects
articles.excerpt_original: As back-end-of-line (BEOL) scaling pushes porous low-k dielectrics toward their reliability limits, nonporous dielectrics that combine a low dielectric constant (k) with mechanical, thermal, and interfacial robustness are increasingly needed. Among nonporous low-k candidates, amorphous boron nitride (aBN) has attracted attention for advanced BEOL interconnects owing to its low-k value (k ≈ 2) and high mechanical robustness, as reflected by a Young's modulus of ~50 GPa. In this review, we discuss aBN from a BEOL process-integration perspective, focusing on the origin of its low-k behavior, process-dependent structure-property relationships, and its potential roles in BEOL interconnects and hybrid-bonding interfaces. Finally, we discuss remaining issues and future directions for validating aBN as a nonporous low-k dielectric/interface material under BEOL and hybrid-bonding integration.
articles.summary_en: A review examines amorphous boron nitride as a nonporous low-k dielectric for next-generation back-end-of-line interconnects. With a dielectric constant near 2 and Young’s modulus of about 50 GPa, the material may improve mechanical and interfacial robustness, though integration validation remains necessary.

articles.title_original: Data and Mathematica notebooks supporting "Nonlinear phononic slidetronics"
articles.title_en: Data support light-driven switching in bilayer h-BN
articles.excerpt_original: This dataset contains the first-principles calculation data and Mathematica notebooks supporting the study of light-driven phonon dynamics and ferroelectric switching in bilayer hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN), as presented in the accompanying manuscript and Supplemental Material. The deposit includes density functional theory (DFT) total energies, structural and phonon information, dielectric-response data, fitted coupling coefficients, and Mathematica notebooks used to calculate potential-energy landscapes and simulate light-driven switching between the oppositely polarized AB and BA stacking configurations. Potential-energy landscape The notebook 2DPotential_energy_landscape.nb processes DFT total energies calculated for different amplitudes of the two interlayer shear modes, Q₄ and Q₅. It constructs the two-dimensional potential-energy surface V(Q₄, Q₅), extracts selected one-dimensional energy profiles, and identifies minimum-energy configurations and switching pathways. The corresponding energy data are provided in Vasp_datafiles/energy.dat. These calculations generate Fig. 1 of the main manuscript. Light-driven phonon dynamics and switching The notebook All_mechanism.nb contains the interaction potentials, equations of motion, and numerical simulations for six excitation mechanisms: Infrared-active excitation; Ionic Raman scattering (IRS); Impulsive stimulated Raman scattering (ISRS); THz sum-frequency excitation (THz-SFE); Infrared resonant Raman scattering (IRRS); Dynamical tilting of the double-well potential. Depending on the mechanism, the notebook calculates the applied electric-field pulse, time-dependent phonon amplitudes, trajectories in phonon-coordinate space, dynamically modified double-well potentials, and switching between AB and BA stacking. It gene
articles.summary_en: An OpenAlex dataset provides first-principles calculations and Mathematica notebooks for studying light-driven phonon dynamics and ferroelectric switching between AB and BA stacking in bilayer hexagonal boron nitride. The work models multiple excitation mechanisms, including infrared, Raman, and terahertz pathways, supporting research into nonlinear phononic slidetronics.

articles.title_original: Semiconductor Protection Area: 2D Layout Designs with 3D Thermal-Mechanical Elasto-Plastic Simulations
articles.title_en: 2D Semiconductor Protection Designs Evaluated with 3D Thermal-Mechanical Simulations
articles.excerpt_original: The protection area surrounding a semiconductor chip guards its circuit against thermal-mechanical defects induced during wafer dicing.The dataset contains 110k designs (across 18 metal stacks of a dummy technology node) governed by 2D manufacturing constraints and evaluated with thermal-mechanical quasi-static structural analysis using 3D finite element method. The resulting sequential thermal-mechanical stress fields, which correspond to the physical states during manufacturing processes, enable two key cross-dimensional benchmarks for machine learning: design-to-stress forward problem, and stress-to-design inverse problem.
articles.summary_en: Researchers analyzed 110,000 semiconductor protection-area designs across 18 metal stacks using 3D finite-element thermal-mechanical simulations. The resulting stress-field dataset supports machine-learning benchmarks for predicting manufacturing stresses from layouts and reconstructing layouts from stress patterns.

articles.title_original: Wafer Scale Solution Processing of 2D Transistors and Circuits With High Mobility Single‐Flake Transport
articles.title_en: Dielectrophoretic Assembly Enables Wafer-Scale Single-Flake MoS₂ Transistors
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Solution‐processed 2D semiconductor‐based thin film transistors (TFTs) offer a pathway to achieve flexible and large‐area electronics. However, their performance is typically limited by the inter‐flake resistance that masks the intrinsic electronic properties of these materials. This is because conventional hydrodynamics‐driven solution deposition techniques lack precise flake placement ability, and result in a stochastic multi‐flake network, leading to low device mobility and large variability. Here, we demonstrate that dielectrophoretic assembly can precisely align 2D MoS 2 flakes from an ultra‐low‐concentration dispersion (1.2 µg mL −1 ) into predefined channel regions, resulting in high mobility single‐flake transport. This approach enables assembly of 16,000 devices on a 3‐inch wafer with >97% yield. With printed electrolyte gating, these fully solution‐processed TFTs show an average On/Off ratio > 10 6 and device mobility of 51 cm 2 V −1 s −1 . Further, they demonstrate excellent stability under switching operations, electrical bias‐stress, and dynamic mechanical tests. When compared with the multi‐flake devices, the single‐flake architecture delivers more than a fourfold increase in device mobility. The concept has also been validated by fabricating functional logic gates and circuits. This generic approach to fabricate large‐area, single‐flake TFTs with low variability establishes a pathway for high‐performance, scalable solution‐processed 2D electronics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated solution-processed MoS₂ transistors assembled on a 3-inch wafer, producing 16,000 devices with over 97% yield. Single-flake transport improved mobility more than fourfold versus multi-flake devices, supporting scalable flexible electronics and logic circuits.

articles.title_original: Structural Engineering and Molecular Doping Strategies to Enhance Electrical Conductivity in Organic Semiconductors for Superior Thermoelectric Performance
articles.title_en: Review Highlights Molecular Strategies for Higher-Performance Organic Thermoelectrics
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT A significant portion of produced energy is dissipated as heat, making it crucial to find ways to capture and reuse it. Organic thermoelectric (OTE) materials have emerged as promising contenders in this field owing to their molecular engineering properties, low thermal conductivity, tunable electronic characteristics, lightweight nature, and compatibility with flexible substrates. While these advantages are notable, improving the electrical conductivity remains critical for achieving efficient thermoelectric performance. This review comprehensively scrutinizes recent advances in OTE materials, highlighting strategies such as backbone and sidechain engineering, heteroatom substitution, solvent and acid treatments, ionic modifications, organic and inorganic dopants. Apart from carbon nanostructure hybrids, this review highlights effective ways to improve electrical conductivity without compromising the Seebeck coefficient. It provides insights into future research directions aimed at advancing cost‐effective, high‐performance organic thermoelectric technologies.
articles.summary_en: A review examines backbone and side-chain engineering, heteroatom substitution, chemical treatments, ionic modification, and organic or inorganic doping to improve electrical conductivity in organic thermoelectric materials. These approaches target efficient heat recovery while preserving flexibility, low thermal conductivity, and favorable Seebeck coefficients.

articles.title_original: Substitutional Mn dimers in graphene created by ultralow-energy cluster-ion implantation
articles.title_en: Substitutional Manganese Dimers Created in Graphene by Ultralow-Energy Ion Implantation
articles.summary_en: Researchers report creating substitutional manganese dimers in graphene using ultralow-energy cluster-ion implantation. The work advances control of atomic dopants in graphene, but no specific commercial application is identified.

articles.title_original: Defect-Engineered PECVD-Grown hBN Enabling Effective Charge Trapping in IGZO Synaptic Transistors
articles.title_en: Defect-Engineered hBN Improves Charge Trapping in IGZO Synaptic Transistors
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Neuromorphic devices require reliable charge trapping mechanisms to emulate synaptic functionalities such as hysteresis, memory retention, and weight modulation; however, conventional oxide semiconductor-based devices often suffer from limited stability due to the absence of well-defined trapping layers. Here, we demonstrate that defect-engineered hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) grown by plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD) can serve as an effective charge-trapping interlayer in indium-gallium-zinc oxide (IGZO) synaptic transistors. The PECVD-grown hBN exhibits significant structural disorder, oxygen-related bonding, increased Urbach energy, and reduced film density, indicating the presence of abundant defect-induced localized states that provide energetically favorable sites for charge trapping and retention. When the hBN film is integrated with the IGZO semiconducting channel layer, it significantly enhances the charge trapping efficiency, resulting in a pronounced increase in the hysteresis window from 0.8 to 4.7 V, along with improved synaptic characteristics such as enhanced potentiation/depression behavior and stable long-term memory retention. These results highlight the potential of PECVD-grown defect-rich hBN as a functional charge-trapping layer for high-performance oxide semiconductor-based neuromorphic devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate PECVD-grown, defect-rich hexagonal boron nitride as a charge-trapping interlayer in IGZO neuromorphic transistors. The layer increased the hysteresis window from 0.8 to 4.7 V and supported improved synaptic behavior and long-term memory retention.

articles.title_original: Ab initio modelling of photoinduced electron dynamics in nanostructures
articles.title_en: Hybrid modelling of photoinduced electron dynamics in TMD–nanoparticle systems
articles.excerpt_original: Nanostructured materials have recently attracted much interest due to their unique properties which make them appealing for the next generation of efficient and novel optical/electrical devices. In particular, two-dimensional (atomically thin) materials such as transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have been extensively researched and shown to exhibit, e.g., strong optical absorption when compared to their bulk counterparts, with potential applications in photovoltaics for solar energy. The optical absorption in such materials may be further improved by decoration with metal nanoparticles (MNPs) due to a plasmonic enhancement effect. While such an effect has been demonstrated experimentally, it is hard to show theoretically from an ab initio point of view due to the computational demand of such calculations: the state-of- the-art approaches commonly used to determine the optical spectra of, e.g, the semiconducting TMD (i.e. density functional theory (DFT) and many-body perturbation theory) may not be applied to the full TMD-MNP structure as the MNP is often on a much larger scale than the semiconductor rendering the ab initio methods infeasible. In this thesis, we develop a dynamical, hybrid approach (the projected equations of motion (PEOM) method) where a composite material is split into subsystems which are then coupled electromagnetically. The primary system (e.g., the TMD) may be treated using any time- dependent theory, while the secondary system (e.g., the MNP) is modelled entirely through its frequency-dependent polarisability which is fitted to obtain parameters which enter into the PEOMs. As a proof of concept, the PEOM method is first applied to a semiconducting quantum dot- MNP system and the obtained energy absorption rates and population dynamics are com
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a projected equations of motion approach to model optical absorption and electron dynamics in composite systems combining two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides with metal nanoparticles. The method addresses the computational limitations of applying ab initio techniques to structures with nanoparticles much larger than the semiconductor.

articles.title_en: Laser-controlled reduction tunes graphene oxide films with subnanometer precision
articles.excerpt_original: Graphene oxide is a promising two-dimensional material with potential applications in many areas. It is basically a graphene basal plane decorated with various oxygen functional groups. By removing the functional groups through reduction, graphene oxide can be reduced to graphene-like films, hence it is an important precursor in industry for the mass fabrication of graphene products. Through reduction, a wide range of properties (optical, electrical, chemical and many others) of graphene oxide can be readily tuned, making it a highly versatile material in nanoscience and technology. This thesis reports original research work on laser-controlled reduction of individual graphene oxide films. Single flakes of graphene oxide film ranging from one to seven layers were reduced with controlled laser irradiation. Functional groups were removed by the heat generated from laser irradiation. The reduction can be controlled under such a precise way that the film thickness can be accurately thinned with sub-nm steps. This allows tailor-making the properties of the films and custom-designing the functionality of nanodevices with on-demand properties. articles.summary_en: Academic research demonstrates laser-induced reduction of one- to seven-layer graphene oxide films, removing oxygen groups through localized heating. The process enables subnanometer thickness control and precise tuning of work function for customized nanodevice functionality.

articles.title_original: Parafermions in fractional Chern insulator-superconductor heterostructures: the role of spin polarization
articles.title_en: Polarized graphene heterostructures could host Z3 parafermions
articles.excerpt_original: Most proposals for $Z_3$ parafermions in fractional quantum Hall-superconductor structures used the spin-unpolarized $ν= 2/3$ Halperin $(1,1,2)$ state. The fractional quantum anomalous Hall (FQAH) states of twisted MoTe$_2$ and rhombohedral graphene are believed to be spin- and valley-polarized Jain states, with the same topological order but a different spin structure. We analyze a trench between two polarized $ν= 2/3$ edges. Among the pairing and tunneling bilinears of the edge-mode electrons, exactly two of each have zero conformal spin. Pairing is compatible only with the neutral-mode superconductivity channel and tunneling only with neutral-mode backscattering, whereas in the unpolarized state singlet pairing and tunneling select the same channel. Since the two channels condense the same neutral anyon up to a local operator, the domain walls carry $Z_3$ parafermions, with 3 protected states per pair, whether or not the neutral channel changes between regions; fixing the fermion parity does not enlarge this count. Before the neutral gap forms, pairing is at best marginal for repulsive inter-edge coupling unless an attractive neutral coupling favors its channel; once the gap has formed, both charge terms are relevant for an inter-edge Coulomb coupling below 7/25 of the intra-edge one. The superconductor must supply even-frequency, equal-spin, intravalley pairing, which an s-wave singlet superconductor with only Ising spin-orbit coupling does not provide at leading order, whereas chiral $p+ip$ and $f+if$ states do. The $Z_3$ label is carried by a quasiparticle of the FQAH state, so no process confined to a junction whose tunneling segments are not FQAH can change it, and we expect a $6π$-periodic Josephson current with or without fixed fermion parity.
articles.summary_en: Theoretical analysis finds that polarized fractional Chern insulator–superconductor interfaces in rhombohedral graphene can support Z3 parafermions with three protected states per pair. Realizing the proposed phase requires even-frequency, equal-spin, intravalley pairing, potentially from chiral p+ip or f+if superconductors, and could produce a 6π-periodic Josephson effect.

articles.title_original: Electrochemical synthesis of graphene oxide from powdered graphitic materials
articles.title_en: Electrochemical Process Produces Graphene Oxide from Graphite Powder
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract An electrochemical route for synthesizing graphene oxide (GO) from powdered graphite was investigated. Previous electrochemical GO syntheses have mainly used graphite sheets or foils; when powdered graphite has been used, the powder generally had to be packed in a porous container or compressed to maintain electrical contact, which often limited oxidation efficiency and yield. Here, expanded graphite powder was molded into a self-supporting sheet with a PVDF binder and subjected to a two-step electrochemical process consisting of sulfate intercalation in concentrated sulfuric acid followed by oxidation in diluted sulfuric acid. After purification, GO was obtained in >70% carbon-based yield. The high yield is attributed to the molded structure, which balanced electrolyte/water transport with electronic conduction. In addition, the mild two-step protocol suppressed the detachment of insufficiently oxidized graphite caused by gas evolution at high voltage. Raman, atomic force microscopy, x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and electron microscopy analyses indicated that the product consisted primarily of monolayer to few-layer GO with preserved graphene domains.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a two-step electrochemical method that molds expanded graphite powder into a self-supporting PVDF-bound sheet, improving electrical contact and transport during oxidation. The process produced primarily mono- to few-layer graphene oxide at more than 70% carbon-based yield, indicating a potentially useful alternative to sheet- or foil-based synthesis.

articles.title_original: Quantum materials QED with van der Waals crystals
articles.title_en: Graphene–hBN Cavities Enable Tunable Mid-Infrared Quantum Electrodynamics
articles.excerpt_original: A central goal of the emerging field of materials QED is to harness subwavelength electromagnetic confinement in engineered cavities to tailor light-matter interactions. Here, we demonstrate that van der Waals multilayer cavities composed of stacked graphene and hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) provide unprecedented control over hybridization between their electromagnetic resonances. By magnetically tuning graphene inter-Landau-level transitions (ILTs) into resonance with hBN phonons, we witness broadband, mode-selective strong coupling in the mid-infrared. Our quantum-material QED framework shows that cavity geometry and layer placement jointly control both coupling strength and modal selectivity. For experimentally realistic cavity parameters, the predicted mode splitting exceeds the width of the hBN Reststrahlen band, providing a direct route to the ultrastrong coupling regime. Together, these results establish van der Waals multilayer cavities as a scalable platform for tunable multimode QED and broaden the design space for reconfigurable quantum materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate that stacked graphene and hexagonal boron nitride crystals can strongly couple graphene inter-Landau-level transitions with hBN phonons. The work establishes a scalable platform for tunable multimode quantum electrodynamics and potential ultrastrong light–matter coupling.

articles.title_original: Nonvolatile reversible ferroelectric controlled half-metallicity of 2D room-temperature ferromagnetic heterostructures CrSF/Sc2CO2
articles.title_en: Ferroelectric control enables reversible half-metallicity in 2D magnetic heterostructures
articles.excerpt_original: Nonvolatile electrical manipulation of two-dimensional van der Waals (vdW) magnets represents an important emerging research direction for spintronic devices. In this work, we utilize first-principles computations to thoroughly characterize the intrinsic magnetoelectric properties of the vertical CrSF/Sc2CO2 heterostructures assembled from ferromagnetic CrSF and ferroelectric Sc2CO2 semiconductors. We demonstrate that the transition between half-metallic and semiconducting states can be effectively modulated by changing the ferroelectric polarization of the Sc2CO2 layer, driven mainly by interlayer charge transfer. This transition implies a substantial change in the electronic transport behavior, as the half-metallic state provides a metallic conduction channel while the semiconducting state retains a finite bandgap. Remarkably, the CrSF/Sc2CO2 vdW heterostructure retains far surpass room temperature ferromagnetism under both ferroelectric polarization configurations. The present study establishes a feasible modulation strategy to realize nonvolatile electrical regulation for developing next-generation low-power spintronic memory devices.
articles.summary_en: First-principles calculations show that CrSF/Sc₂CO₂ heterostructures can switch nonvolatily between half-metallic and semiconducting states through ferroelectric polarization. The structures retain above-room-temperature ferromagnetism, suggesting a route toward low-power spintronic memory devices.

articles.title_original: Sodium Adsorption and Mobility in a Pillared Graphene Structure
articles.title_en: Pillared Graphene Evaluated for Sodium-Ion Battery Anodes
articles.excerpt_original: Sodium-ion batteries are generally considered a promising alternative to lithium-ion batteries due to the abundance and low cost of sodium. However, their main limitation is the lack of an appropriate anode, since the usual graphite electrode used in lithium batteries is incompatible with the larger ionic radius of sodium. In this work, the theoretical behavior of pillared graphene as a possible anode is analyzed via computational simulations based on Density Functional Theory (DFT) using the FIREBALL program. The structural relaxation results reveal that staggered pillars are more stable than the aligned alternative. The adsorption energy of sodium is shown to be significantly higher than for graphite, with a maximum value of −2.23 eV, leading to an important energetic benefit. The diffusion analysis shows high mobility for sodium, with migration barriers comparable to those of lithium ions both in the flat regions of the structure and close to the nanotubes. The values are comparable to those of the standard graphite used in current batteries. Finally, the charge analysis confirms significant electronic transfer from both sodium and lithium to the lattice. These data indicate that pillared graphene can be a good candidate for the optimization of charge dynamics in sodium-ion batteries.
articles.summary_en: Computational simulations indicate that pillared graphene offers stronger sodium adsorption and high ion mobility, with diffusion barriers comparable to those of lithium in graphite. The findings identify the structure as a potential anode material for improving sodium-ion battery charge dynamics.

articles.title_original: MXenes: Types, preparation, and applications in water treatment
articles.title_en: MXene Membranes for Water Treatment: Materials, Design and Scale-Up Challenges
articles.excerpt_original: MXenes have attracted significant attention as advanced 2D materials for water treatment, but previous assessments have been largely descriptive and have not adequately compared material types, manufacturing strategies, and practical performance. This paper aims to evaluate MXene-based membranes in terms of composition, surface chemistry, interlayer engineering and membrane design and to relate properties to water flux, rejection efficiency, adsorption capacity, antifouling behaviour and stability. Our goal is not to provide general summaries, but to highlight the critical points that will guide MXenes from laboratory demonstrations to real-world applications in water purification. This review also addresses major challenges including oxidation, restacking, swelling, mechanical fragility, scalability and environmental safety. Such a contrast between existing gaps and present advances provides a more lucid basis for the selection and design of MXene membranes in sustainable water treatment applications.

articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Colloidal quantum dot (CQD) infrared (IR) photodetectors exhibit great application potential in the fields of optical communication, environmental monitoring, imaging, and wearable sensing. Specifically, AgBiS2 CQD IR photodetectors have garnered extensive attention because of their excellent photoelectric properties, solution-processability, as well as non-toxicity and environmental friendliness. However, the high trap density and relatively low carrier mobility of AgBiS2 CQDs have limited their development in high-performance IR photodetectors. Herein, a representative 2D transition carbide, Ti3C2Tx, is introduced into the AgBiS2 CQD films to develop enhanced IR photodetectors based on MXene/AgBiS2 hybrid films. By finely controlling of the MXene additive concentration, this combination possibly helps reduce trap state density in AgBiS2 films to suppress carrier nonradiative recombination and simultaneously constructs an efficient conductive pathway in AgBiS2 films to enhance the extraction of photo-generated carriers. Consequently, compared to the pristine AgBiS2 CQD devices, the MXene/AgBiS2 CQD-based infrared photodetector exhibits significant promotion in the responsivity, EQE, and estimated normalized detectivity under a broad band from 500 to 900 nm, demonstrating an alternative method for tailoring the performance of AgBiS2 CQD optoelectronic devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers introduced Ti3C2Tx MXene nanoflakes into AgBiS2 colloidal quantum-dot films to reduce trap density and improve carrier extraction. The hybrid devices showed improved responsivity, external quantum efficiency, and estimated detectivity across 500–900 nm, supporting applications in infrared sensing and optoelectronics.

articles.title_original: MXene electrocatalysts for hydrogen evolution and methanol oxidation: Interfacial mechanisms, architectures, and emerging design principles for energy-saving electrolysis

articles.excerpt_original: Electrochemical hydrogen production is central to renewable and sustainable energy systems, yet conventional water electrolysis remains limited by the sluggish oxygen evolution reaction, high anodic overpotentials, and associated efficiency losses. Coupling the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) with the methanol oxidation reaction (MOR) offers an energy-saving alternative by replacing oxygen evolution with potentially value-added anodic conversion. In this context, MXenes have emerged as promising electrocatalytic platforms because their metallic conductivity, tunable surface terminations, defect chemistry, and strong interfacial interactions enable regulation of adsorption energetics, charge redistribution, and local reaction microenvironments. This review critically examines MXene electrocatalysts for HER and MOR, with emphasis on interfacial mechanisms, catalyst architectures, and emerging design principles for energy-saving electrolysis. Cross-cutting comparisons show how termination and interlayer control, defect and coordination engineering, atom or cluster anchoring, and heterostructure construction regulate hydrogen adsorption, water activation, interfacial charge transfer, carbonaceous-intermediate conversion, and poisoning resistance. For MOR, particular attention is given to the distinction between activity or CO-tolerance evidence and quantitative product analysis, because high anodic current alone does not establish selective value-added conversion. articles.summary_en: This review examines MXene catalysts for hydrogen evolution coupled with methanol oxidation, highlighting how surface terminations, defects, interlayer structure and heterostructures influence activity and durability. It also identifies challenges including catalyst degradation, methanol crossover and inconsistent testing protocols.

articles.title_original: Recent advances in boron containing anticancer drug delivery nanocarrier platforms
articles.title_en: Boron Nanocarriers Advance Targeted Anticancer Drug Delivery
articles.excerpt_original: Boron-containing compounds have emerged as versatile building blocks in the design of advanced anticancer drug delivery systems due to their unique chemical features, including electron deficiency, reversible covalent interactions, and structural diversity. In recent years, significant progress has been made in engineering boron-functionalized nanocarriers to enhance tumor targeting, improve drug loading efficiency, and achieve controlled release while minimizing systemic toxicity. This review highlights recent advances in boron-containing anticancer drug delivery nanoplatforms, including boron-nitride nanoparticles, boronic acid-functionalized polymers, BODIPY-based nanocarriers and boron incorporated supramolecular nanoplatforms. Particular attention is given to stimulus-responsive systems exploiting the dynamic covalent interactions between boronic acids and cis-diols for pH-, ligand-, or reactive oxygen species-triggered drug release in the tumor microenvironment. Strategies to improve cellular uptake, enhance intracellular stability, and achieve selective cytotoxicity are also discussed. Furthermore, multifunctional nanocarriers incorporating imaging capabilities or combinatorial therapeutic modalities are examined. Despite promising preclinical results, challenges remain in large-scale production, long-term biosafety evaluation, pharmacokinetic optimization, and clinical translation. Overall, boron- containing nanocarriers represent a rapidly evolving platform with strong potential to advance targeted and responsive anticancer drug delivery.
articles.summary_en: A review surveys boron-containing nanocarriers, including boron-nitride nanoparticles, boronic acid-functionalized polymers, BODIPY systems, and supramolecular platforms, for targeted and stimulus-responsive cancer therapy. Despite promising preclinical results, scale-up, biosafety, pharmacokinetics, and clinical translation remain challenges.

articles.title_original: Machine Learning for Hydrogen Storage in Boron‐Based Materials: Key Descriptors and Data Constraints
articles.title_en: Machine Learning Identifies Key Descriptors for Boron-Based Hydrogen Storage
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT The transition to a sustainable energy economy critically depends on the development of safe, efficient, and cost‐effective hydrogen storage solutions. Boron‐based materials are promising solid‐state hydrogen storage candidates with high gravimetric capacity, but their use remains limited by kinetic and thermodynamic challenges. This study employs a data‐driven approach with machine learning (ML) to systematically analyze the structure–property–performance relationships in these systems. A curated dataset comprising 1073 experimental entries from 20 articles (2000–2023) was analyzed using regularized linear regression (Ridge, Lasso, and Elastic Net), random forest (RF), and gradient boosting (GB) algorithms, using an article‐wise cross‐validation scheme that kept all data from the same publication within a single fold, preventing information leakage. The linear models were unable to describe the adsorption behavior adequately, and expanding the descriptor set did not improve them, indicating an intrinsic limitation of the linear formulation. The nonlinear ensembles performed clearly better, indicating that the underlying relationships are nonlinear, though their overall accuracy was still modest. Despite its greater complexity, GB did not outperform RF, which is likely related to the outlier‐prone and uneven distribution of the data. SHAP analysis showed that both ensembles identified the same leading descriptors, namely the preparation method and adsorption pressure, followed by temperature, surface area, and boron and carbon content. The direction of their effects agreed with known adsorption behavior. articles.summary_en: A machine-learning study analyzed 1,073 experimental records to model hydrogen adsorption in boron-based materials. Random-forest and gradient-boosting models captured nonlinear relationships, while incomplete reporting of surface area and pore volume constrained predictive accuracy.

articles.title_original: Non-volatile memristors as prospective radio frequency switches for 6G communications - A review
articles.title_en: Review Assesses Non-Volatile Memristors for 6G RF Switching
articles.excerpt_original: As communication technologies continue to improve to the 6G standard, highly performing radio frequency (RF) switches that have short switching times, high energy efficiency, high cutoff frequencies, capabilities of operating beyond 100 GHz while maintaining reasonable RF performance, and high data transmission rates of 100 Gbit s −1 are needed. Existing RF switches based on solid-state and microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) technologies fall short of meeting these requirements because of their volatility and parasitic inductive effects that lead to undesirably high insertion losses at high frequencies. Non-volatile memristors are emerging as likely candidates to replace traditional switches. They offer numerous benefits, including virtually zero static energy consumption, fast switching speeds, and excellent scalability. This review will provide an overview of the progress and challenges associated with implementing four types of non-volatile memristive technologies as RF switches: Resistive random access memory (ReRAM), conductive bridge random access memory (CBRAM), phase change memory (PCM), and memory based on two-dimensional (2D) materials, specifically molybdenum disulfide (MoS 2 ) and hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). The performance of these prospective switches is compared against one another and subsequently benchmarked against existing switch technologies. The review will provide an objective critique of the future readiness for 6G for the four main types of memristive switch technologies based on factors such as RF performance, CMOS compatibility, and fabrication maturity.
