articles.summary_en: A finite-element and machine-learning study proposes an MXene interfacial layer in a Cs₂AgBiBr₆ lead-free perovskite solar cell, with modeled broadband absorption above 80% and power-conversion efficiency of 22.84%. The work compares MXene favorably with graphene for optical absorption, current density, and efficiency, but reports simulation results rather than demonstrated device performance.

articles.title_original: Numerical investigation of Sulfamoylbenzoic acid-functionalized MXene interface modifier for high efficiency perovskite solar cells
articles.title_en: MXene Interlayer Modeling Targets Higher-Efficiency Perovskite Solar Cells
articles.excerpt_original: In the pursuit of sustainable, high-efficiency energy solutions, perovskite (PVT) solar cells (PSCs) have emerged as promising candidates due to their tunable optoelectronic properties and low-cost fabrication. However, commercialization remains hindered by efficiency stagnation and interfacial instability, particularly at the buried electron transport layer (ETL)/PVT interface. To address this, a novel interfacial modification strategy is proposed using MXene functionalized with 4-sulfamoylbenzoic acid (MX-Sba) as an interlayer at the ETL/PVT junction in cesiumformamidinium (CsFAMAPbIBr2)-based PSCs. The carboxylic acid-terminated MX-Sba improves conductivity, energy level alignment, and defect passivation, facilitating efficient charge extraction and reduced non-radiative recombination. Numerical simulations revealed favorable band bending, charge carrier mobility, and interfacial transport characteristics. A detailed analysis underscores the impact of interfacial defect density and resistance variations on charge dynamics and device performance. The optimized device exhibits a remarkable power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 25.15%, with a short circuit current density (J sc ) of 24.35 mA/cm 2 , open circuit voltage (V oc ) of 1.262 V, and fill factor (FF) of 81.81%. articles.summary_en: Numerical simulations indicate that sulfamoylbenzoic acid-functionalized MXene can improve conductivity, band alignment and defect passivation at the electron-transport-layer/perovskite interface. articles.title_original: Nonlinear Quantum Waves in Semiconductor Superlattices
articles.title_en: Review Connects Nonlinear Semiconductor Waves to Twisted Bilayer Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Semiconductor superlattices constitute an ideal laboratory for investigating coherent electron dynamics and nonlinear charge transport in periodic nanostructures. Their miniband electronic structure gives rise to Bloch oscillations, Wannier-Stark localization, resonant tunneling, electric-field domain formation, and self-sustained current oscillations over a wide range of temporal and spatial scales. This article reviews the multiscale theoretical framework developed to describe these phenomena, from semiclassical Boltzmann-Poisson-BGK kinetic equations to fully quantum Wigner-Poisson formulations. It shows how systematic asymptotic analysis bridges microscopic quantum kinetics and macroscopic nonlinear transport. Systematic hydrodynamic reductions yield generalized and quantum drift-diffusion equations that retain the essential effects of scattering, self-consistent electrostatics, coherent tunneling, and quantum interference while remaining amenable to analytical investigation and efficient numerical simulation. These reduced descriptions account for Gunn-type oscillations mediated by traveling waves, the coexistence of Bloch and Gunn oscillations under appropriate conditions, and nonlinear transport involving multiple minibands. The review concludes by discussing how the methodology developed for semiconductor superlattices may be extended to emerging quantum materials, including moire superlattices, twisted bilayer graphene, Floquet-engineered systems, and topological materials, where Berry curvature, quantum geometry, orbital magnetic moments, and strong electronic correlations enrich the dynamics of coherent quantum waves.
articles.summary_en: This review develops multiscale kinetic, hydrodynamic, and quantum descriptions of coherent transport phenomena in semiconductor superlattices. It identifies twisted bilayer graphene and other emerging quantum materials as potential extensions where Berry curvature, quantum geometry, and electronic correlations may shape nonlinear wave dynamics.

articles.title_original: Size-Effect and Defect Sensitivity in Nano-Structures and Graphene Components
articles.title_en: Size Effects and Defect Sensitivity in Graphene Structural Components
articles.excerpt_original: nano-materials, such as graphene and carbon nanotubes, into large-scale structural engineering represents a revolutionary shift toward ultra-lightweight and hyper-strong systems. On a microscopic scale, these materials possess extraordinary tensile strength and elastic modulus, promising structures like space elevators or hyper-span bridges. However, scaling these materials from the micrometer level to macroscopic structural elements introduces a profound mechanical dilemma known as the "size-effect" and heightened defect sensitivity. The core engineering dilemma is that as the physical volume of the structural component increases, the probability of incorporating microscopic lattice defects, vacancies, or misalignments grows exponentially. In conventional materials like structural steel, local yielding allows for stress redistribution around minor flaws. In contrast, pristine nano-composites are highly brittle and lack this plastic redistribution capacity. A single microscopic defect within a large-scale graphene-infused beam can act as a severe stress concentrator, initiating an instantaneous, catastrophic fracture that propagates across the entire element at the speed of sound. Consequently, the material's structural capacity drops drastically as its physical dimensions scale up, rendering terrestrial micro-scale test data completely unrepresentative of macro-scale structural behavior. Developing statistical fracture mechanics models and manufacturing techniques that can guarantee structural reliability in macro-scale nano-structures remains an unresolved barrier.
articles.summary_en: The research discusses how defect probability and brittle fracture behavior can limit the scalability of graphene-infused structural components. It identifies statistical fracture-mechanics modelling and reliable large-scale manufacturing as unresolved requirements for structural applications.

articles.title_original: Probing hydrodynamics in graphene and quark matter via Seebeck coefficient
articles.title_en: Study Probes Hydrodynamic Transport in Graphene Using the Seebeck Coefficient
articles.excerpt_original: We investigate the Seebeck coefficient as a probe of collective transport behavior in graphene and quark-gluon plasma using a kinetic-theory approach in the hydrodynamic regime. The Seebeck coefficient is obtained by solving the Boltzmann transport equation in the relaxation-time approximation. At high-charge-carrier density, corresponding to the Fermi-liquid domain, our result approaches the behavior expected from the conventional Mott relation. In contrast, significant deviations from the Mott relation are observed in the low-carrier-density regime, corresponding to the Dirac fluid domain. These facts are in good agreement with experimental Seebeck coefficient data for graphene. This behavior indicates the emergence of collective hydrodynamic transport in graphene. The enthalpy per particle plays a key role for the Seebeck coefficient in the Dirac fluid regime. We extend our formalism to the ultra-relativistic quark-gluon plasma. A similar deviation from the Mott relation is observed, supporting a similar fluid response in the Seebeck coefficient across two markedly different strongly correlated quantum systems - graphene and quark matter.
articles.summary_en: Researchers use kinetic theory to examine how graphene’s Seebeck coefficient reflects collective hydrodynamic transport. The study identifies deviations from the conventional Mott relation in the low-carrier-density Dirac-fluid regime, consistent with experimental data, while comparing the behavior with quark matter.

articles.title_original: Capacitance sensing in bilayer graphene with gate reflectometry
articles.title_en: Gate Reflectometry Enables Capacitance Sensing in Bilayer Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: In the search for topological states in bilayer graphene, capacitance measurement methods are widely utilized in bridge type readouts or source-drain reflectometry setups. In this paper we demonstrate an alternative readout method based on gate reflectometry. We probe the capacitance of a BLG flake encapsulated between hBN and WSe$_2$ through a lumped-element LC resonator coupled to the top gate electrode of the heterostructure. The microwave readout reliably tracks the opening of a displacement field-induced band gap in the device. Compared to simultaneous DC transport measurements, the RF signal proves to be less affected by the percolating transport channels caused by sample disorder. Furthermore, we use the gate based readout to identify a small-angle alignment between the hBN and BLG flake. From the fixed frequency microwave readout, we extract the device capacitance change between the insulating and metallic state of the bilayer and utilize a comprehensive capacitance network model to explain its origin. Finally, we propose an advanced, multiplexed double-resonator readout scheme capable of simultaneously measuring top and bottom gate capacitances to extract the layer polarizability of the system. This work establishes gate reflectometry as a highly scalable and powerful methodology for exploring topological phases and internal charge dynamics in van der Waals heterostructures.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate microwave gate reflectometry for tracking displacement-field-induced band gaps and capacitance changes in hBN/WSe₂-encapsulated bilayer graphene. The proposed multiplexed double-resonator approach could support scalable probing of topological phases and charge dynamics in van der Waals heterostructures.

articles.title_original: Intercalation-assisted remote epitaxy of GaN on epitaxial graphene
articles.title_en: Intercalation Enables Remote Epitaxy of GaN on Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Metalorganic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD) of GaN on pristine epitaxial graphene formed on SiC is hindered by the low energy van der Waals surface, which suppresses nucleation and promotes island growth. Here, we demonstrate an intercalation-assisted approach to modify the graphene/SiC interface and influence GaN nucleation behavior via a remote epitaxy process. Using a pulsed MOCVD technique, a ∼4 nm GaN interlayer was first intercalated beneath the epitaxial graphene followed by subsequent epitaxial growth of the GaN film. Intercalation promotes a high nucleation density, enabling the growth of a coalesced 1.5 μm-thick epitaxial GaN film with step-flow morphology. Cross-sectional scanning transmission electron microscopy reveals atomic alignment between the GaN epilayer and the intercalated GaN across the graphene interlayer, maintaining epitaxial registry. The weak interfacial bonding enables mechanical exfoliation of the GaN film to form a thin, freestanding membrane. These results demonstrate that intercalation can provide an alternative pathway to engineer the graphene/substrate interface to facilitate remote epitaxy without the need for graphene layer transfer.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated intercalation-assisted remote epitaxy to grow a coalesced, 1.5 μm-thick GaN film on epitaxial graphene without transferring the graphene layer. The weak interface enabled mechanical exfoliation of the GaN into a freestanding membrane, supporting potential advances in semiconductor fabrication.

articles.title_original: Enhanced near-field thermal radiation in multilayered hBN-graphene structures without vacuum gaps
articles.title_en: hBN–Graphene Multilayers Enhance Near-Field Thermal Radiation
articles.excerpt_original: Near-field thermal radiation enables heat transport that greatly exceeds the blackbody limit through photon tunneling of evanescent electromagnetic waves at nanoscale separations, and has attracted increasing attention as an alternative heat-dissipation mechanism for miniaturized devices. In this study, we focus on solid-spacer multilayer structures without vacuum gaps, and numerically compare a hyperbolic material, hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), with an isotropic polar material, silicon carbide (SiC), in structures composed of alternating graphene sheets and dielectric spacers. Numerical analysis shows that, at N = 5, the hBN-graphene multilayer structure achieves a total heat flux of 656 kW/m2, approximately 3.0 times that of the SiC-graphene structure (221 kW/m2) under the same conditions, and approximately 6.5 times that of the corresponding vacuum-gap hBN-graphene structure. Analysis of the photon tunneling probability maps reveals that this enhancement originates from hybrid modes formed by coupling between hyperbolic phonon polaritons excited within the Reststrahlen bands of hBN and graphene surface plasmon polaritons. We explicitly identify these hybrid branches in the present vacuum-gap-free, solid-spacer configuration, enabling efficient energy transport through high-wavevector near-field radiative channels. We further confirm that branch splitting of the polaritonic modes associated with multilayering increases the effective density of transmission channels. These results demonstrate that solid-spacer multilayer hBN/graphene structures constitute an effective design strategy for enhancing near-field thermal radiation without requiring vacuum gaps.
articles.summary_en: Numerical analysis shows that solid-spacer hBN–graphene multilayers achieve substantially higher near-field heat flux than comparable SiC–graphene and vacuum-gap structures. Coupled hBN phonon polaritons and graphene plasmons create additional high-wavevector transmission channels, suggesting a route for nanoscale thermal management without vacuum gaps.

articles.title_original: Harnessing Superelasticity for Efficient Load Transfer in NiTi–Graphene Composites
articles.title_en: Superelastic NiTi–Graphene Composites Improve Load Transfer
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Conventional metal–graphene composites cannot fully utilize the high elastic limit of graphene, because metal matrices deform plastically below 1% strain, whereas graphene remains elastic up to 30%. Shape memory alloys such as NiTi accommodate recoverable strains of 8–10% through a stress-induced martensitic transformation, making them well-suited matrices for graphene reinforcement. A ternary second nearest neighbor modified embedded-atom method (2NN MEAM) potential for the Ni–Ti–C system is developed and applied in molecular dynamics simulations of NiTi–graphene composites. The simulations show that the martensitic transformation is preserved and that graphene reinforcement increases the transformation stress in both single-crystal and polycrystalline NiTi. Higher graphene content improves strength but introduces a residual strain that accumulates on cycling. Atomistic analysis shows that this residual strain arises not from a large untransformed matrix fraction, but from irreversible graphene microcracking at peak load, selective matrix intrusion into the crack openings, and localized interfacial martensite trapping. Local transformation stretch tensor analysis shows that reinforcement preserves the B2-to-B19′ path, forming a 50:50 ratio of a (001) compound twin pair continuous across the sheets, with the coherent interfaces showing no preference as nucleation sites. Overall, lattice strain matching enables efficient load transfer to the graphene, enhancing strength while retaining recoverable deformation.
articles.summary_en: Molecular dynamics simulations show that NiTi shape-memory alloys can transfer load to graphene while retaining recoverable deformation through martensitic transformation. Higher graphene content increases strength but causes cycling-related residual strain from graphene microcracking and interfacial effects.

articles.title_original: Designer surface chemistry of two-dimensional MXenes
articles.title_en: Designer Surface Chemistry Advances Expand MXene Applications
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Controlling the surface chemical composition of two-dimensional (2D) transition-metal carbides and nitrides (MXenes) is essential for tailoring their properties. Since 2020, a rapidly growing, community-wide understanding of MXene surface chemistry has transformed the field from handling mixed terminations (–O, –OH, –F, and –Cl) with limited control mechanisms into systematically designing advanced interfaces. However, as we discuss in this issue of MRS Bulletin on MXenes’ surface chemistry, recent breakthroughs in both chemical modification strategies and direct synthesis pathways have unlocked precise substitution, structural editing, and organic–inorganic hybridization of MXenes’ surface as a new metal–organic framework (MOF)-like chemical playground. The articles within this collection aim to serve as a guide to introduce the design concepts behind and novel application directions enabled by MXenes’ surface control and provide a perspective to the field on the areas thatmust be developed to MXenes’ surface chemistry. In addition, this issue aims to spur researchers to address the need for AI-guided predictions in local chemistry and its effects on the relation of composition to properties in surface-controlled MXenes and their eventual best applications. Ultimately, we believe that this emerging “designer era” of MXenes’ surface chemistry will push sophisticated surface engineering as a tool to majorly control MXene’s utility across energy storage, tribology, biointegrated electronics, and other applications far beyond boundaries previously restricted by core-metal chemistry alone.
articles.summary_en: A review highlights new strategies for controlling MXene surface terminations through chemical modification, structural editing, and direct synthesis. The advances could improve MXene performance across energy storage, tribology, and biointegrated electronics, while AI-guided prediction remains a development priority.

articles.title_original: Machine Learning-Assisted Performance Prediction and Design of MXene Materials
articles.title_en: Machine Learning and DFT Advance MXene Materials Design
articles.excerpt_original: MXenes are not a single fixed material family, but a broad set of two-dimensional transition-metal carbides and nitrides. Their conductivity, hydrophilic surfaces, layered structure, and adjustable terminations explain why they are frequently studied for electrocatalysis, energy storage, and multifunctional devices. The same flexibility also makes their design difficult. Changing the metal element, carbide/nitride framework, surface group, defect state, interlayer environment, or heterointerface may alter the final property. Exhaustive trial-and-error experiments or one-by-one DFT calculations are therefore inefficient. In this setting, machine learning (ML) combined with density functional theory (DFT) offers a practical way to screen structures, estimate properties, and narrow the candidate space. Here, reported ML-assisted studies on MXene prediction and design are organized by target property and workflow. The electrocatalysis part covers adsorption free energies, overpotentials, catalytic activity, and complex active sites. The energy-storage part discusses capacity, voltage, capacitance, and electronic-structure descriptors. The later sections examine ML–DFT screening, graph neural networks, uncertainty quantification, active learning, and interpretability. The literature still shows several weak points: small curated datasets, inconsistent data standards, simplified treatment of mixed terminations and defects, and limited transfer across MXene systems. More realistic descriptors, standardized datasets, multi-target screening, interpretable models, and tighter experiment-ML–DFT feedback are needed.
articles.summary_en: A review examines how machine learning combined with density functional theory can predict MXene properties and accelerate screening for electrocatalysis, energy storage, and multifunctional devices. It identifies small datasets, inconsistent standards, and limited transferability as key challenges requiring improved descriptors and experimental validation.

articles.title_original: Doped Non-Ti MXenes for Supercapacitor Applications
articles.title_en: Review Examines Doped Non-Ti MXenes for Supercapacitors
articles.excerpt_original: The rapid development of high-performing energy storage technologies has increased the search for 2D electrode materials with tunable electronic structures, abundant electroactive sites, and rapid ion transportation. Although Ti-based MXenes have been extensively investigated, non-Ti MXenes offer a broader compositional space and distinctive physicochemical properties, yet their supercapacitor applications remain comparatively underexplored. In this review, we critically examine the emerging field of doped non-Ti MXenes for advanced supercapacitor applications, including Mo-, V-, Nb-, Cr-, W-, Zr-, Hf-, Ta-, Sc-, and Y-based systems. In this review, we establish the structural, chemical, and electrochemical characteristics of non-Ti MXenes and subsequently discuss M-, X-, and T-site doping, substitution, and multielement engineering strategies. We have discussed how heteroatom doping regulates electronic structure, charge distribution, defect chemistry, interlayer spacing, surface chemistry, and ion–accessible active sites. These modifications are correlated with their influence on electrochemical kinetics, capacitance, rate capability, and cyclic stability. Finally, computational and data-driven approaches, critical benchmarking, and critical challenges are integrated to establish structure–doping–mechanism–performance relationships and design principles for next-generation doped non-Ti MXene electrodes for supercapacitors.
articles.summary_en: An academic review assesses Mo-, V-, Nb-, Cr-, W-, Zr-, Hf-, Ta-, Sc- and Y-based MXenes for supercapacitor electrodes. It links doping and compositional engineering to electronic structure, ion transport, capacitance, rate capability and cycling stability, while outlining design challenges and computational approaches.

articles.title_original: Three-body amplification based on near-field radiative heat transfer of MXene sheets
articles.title_en: MXene Layers Amplify Near-Field Radiative Heat Transfer
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Near-field radiative heat transfer (NFRHT) in many-body systems offers an effective strategy for enhancing radiative energy transport beyond conventional two-body limits. In this work, the three-body amplification effect in MXene-based systems is systematically investigated by analyzing the influences of the intermediate material, mediator thickness, vacuum gap, photon tunneling behavior, and thermal equilibrium characteristics. The results show that the radiative heat transfer is dominated by TM-polarized evanescent waves throughout the entire parameter range. Among the considered mediators, MXene exhibits the strongest amplification capability. For an ultrathin MXene intermediate layer, the heat flux enhancement factor reaches approximately 1.34 compared with the corresponding two-body configuration, and further increases with vacuum gap, approaching 2.8 at large separations. In contrast, hBN and Ag mediators produce much weaker enhancement effects, while the enhancement provided by SiC remains limited. Spectral heat flux analyses reveal that the energy transfer is primarily concentrated in the low-frequency region associated with MXene surface plasmon polaritons (SPPs). Photon tunneling calculations further demonstrate that the intermediate MXene layer introduces additional SPP-coupling pathways and significantly enlarges the high-transmission region in frequency-wavevector space, allowing more evanescent modes to participate in radiative transport. Furthermore, the steady-state thermal behavior of the intermediate layer confirms the tunability of many-body radiative heat transfer. These findings clarify the physical origin of three-body amplification in MXene systems and highlight the potential of MXene as an efficient mediator for nanoscale thermal managem
articles.summary_en: Researchers show that an ultrathin MXene intermediate layer can enhance near-field radiative heat transfer by approximately 1.34×, rising toward 2.8× at large vacuum gaps. The effect is attributed to additional surface-plasmon-polariton coupling pathways, highlighting MXene’s potential for nanoscale thermal management.

articles.title_original: Design, Functionalities, and Emerging Applications of Ti3C2Tx MXene-Based Composites: A Review
articles.title_en: Review Examines Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene Composite Applications
articles.excerpt_original: The rise of two-dimensional (2D) materials is crucial for advancing modern life and industry. Ti 3 C 2 T x MXenes have attracted significant attention due to their conductivity, natural hydrophilicity, diverse termination groups, and impressive mechanical properties, offering unique advantages in practical applications. When Ti 3 C 2 T x MXene are combined with metal oxide semiconductors and polymers to create functional composites, their applications span multiple fields, including gas sensors, photocatalytic CO 2 reduction, and energy storage. This review will focus on the synthesis methods and physicochemical properties of Ti 3 C 2 T x MXene nanosheets, and will discuss their various applications. Finally, based on the pros and cons of the current research status, the challenges and opportunities for improving MXene-based composites are investigated. This review aims to summarize the latest research results in recent years, offering constructive insights for 2D materials studies.
articles.summary_en: The review surveys Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene synthesis, properties, and composite integration with metal oxides and polymers. It highlights applications in gas sensing, photocatalytic CO₂ reduction, and energy storage while identifying research challenges and opportunities.

articles.title_original: Non-equilibrium surface reconstruction of MXene via nitridation modification for pseudocapacitance-dominated sodium storage
articles.title_en: Nitridation-Modified MXene Enables Pseudocapacitive Sodium Storage
articles.summary_en: Researchers report non-equilibrium surface reconstruction of MXene through nitridation modification to promote pseudocapacitance-dominated sodium storage. The work targets improved electrochemical performance for sodium-based energy-storage systems.

articles.title_original: Steady-state and transient thermal effect of alkane-grafted Ti3C2Tx MXene
articles.title_en: Alkane Grafting Improves MXene Infrared Absorption and Thermal Energy Storage
articles.excerpt_original: Surface functionalization provides an effective strategy for regulating the thermal transport and ultrafast carrier dynamics of MXene materials. However, the underlying coupling mechanism between alkane grafting, phonon scattering, and non-equilibrium energy dissipation remains insufficiently understood. Herein, we investigated the steady-state and transient thermal effects of alkane-grafted Ti3C2Tx MXene thin films through Raman spectroscopy, infrared optical spectroscopy, thermal transport measurements, and femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy. Raman and AFM images demonstrated that long carbon-chain grafting induced enhanced local structural disorder, out-of-plane bending, and edge wrinkling features. Compared with Ti3C2Tx MXene, alkane-grafted Ti3C2Tx-C8H18 and Ti3C2Tx-C12H26 exhibited enhanced infrared absorption together with suppressed thermal transport behavior. In particular, extraction of the absorption coefficient, complex refractive index, and dielectric function further revealed that Ti3C2Tx-C12H26 MXene exhibited the highest average infrared absorptance of approximately 70%, together with an enhanced absorption coefficient, increased imaginary refractive index, and strengthened dielectric loss capability, indicating significantly improved infrared energy dissipation after long-chain alkane grafting. Meanwhile, its thermal diffusivity decreased to 7.57 mm2/s, while the specific heat capacity increased to 1.35 J/(g K), demonstrating its thermal energy storage capability. Femtosecond transient absorption measurements revealed faster carrier relaxation with increasing alkyl-chain length. The fast relaxation component decreased from 4.49 ps for Ti3C2Tx to 2.24 ps for Ti3C2Tx-C12H26. The slow relaxation component also decreased from 1510.86 to 491.26 ps
articles.summary_en: Researchers found that grafting long-chain alkanes onto Ti3C2Tx MXene increased infrared absorptance to approximately 70%, reduced thermal diffusivity, and increased heat capacity. Longer alkyl chains also accelerated carrier relaxation, indicating potential for infrared energy dissipation and thermal-management applications.

articles.title_original: PVA / CS / MXene ‐ LiCl Flexible Material With Multiple Physical Interactions and Ionic‐Electronic Conduction for Strain/Pressure Sensing
articles.title_en: PVA/CS/MXene-LiCl Material Enables Flexible Strain and Pressure Sensing
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Flexible sensors have attracted considerable attention in wearable electronics and health monitoring. However, achieving high mechanical robustness while maintaining effective sensing performance remains challenging for hydrogel‐based flexible sensors, as mechanical reinforcement may compromise sensing sensitivity. Herein, PVA/CS/MXene‐LiCl flexible materials were fabricated through CS doping, LiCl modification, and 100% pre‐stretching treatment, aiming to achieve a favorable balance between mechanical robustness and sensing performance. The optimized PVA/CS/MXene‐LiCl material exhibits excellent mechanical properties with a tensile strength of 1.02 MPa, compressive strength of 2.2 MPa, and toughness of 1.388 MJ/m 3 . Meanwhile, it maintains effective sensing capability, with a conductivity of 174 μS/cm, gauge factors of 0.47 and 0.90 in the strain ranges of 1%–30% and 30%–70%, respectively, and a rapid response/recovery time of 52.1/54 ms. The balanced mechanical and sensing performances are associated with the synergistic integration of the PVA/CS polymer network and the MXene/LiCl ionic‐electronic conductive system. Furthermore, proof‐of‐concept demonstrations show that the flexible material can detect mechanical stimuli ranging from finger bending to subtle pulse and eye‐winking signals. This work demonstrates a simple strategy for integrating mechanical robustness, strain sensing capability, and rapid electromechanical response in PVA‐based flexible sensing materials, providing potential for wearable sensing and human health monitoring.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a PVA/chitosan/MXene-LiCl flexible material combining mechanical robustness with ionic-electronic conductivity. Demonstrations detected bending, pulse, and eye-winking signals, indicating potential for wearable and health-monitoring sensors.

articles.title_original: Effect of Hexagonal Boron Nitride (h-BN) Content on the Mechanical and Tribological Properties of Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM)-Printed PETG Composites
articles.title_en: Low h-BN Content Improves Wear Resistance of 3D-Printed PETG
articles.excerpt_original: PETG composite filaments containing 1 wt%, 3 wt%, and 5 wt% hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) were produced. The produced filaments were transformed into test specimens using the fused deposition modeling (FDM) technique. The tensile, compression, and wear behaviors of the composite polymer test specimens produced by the FDM method were investigated. The wear characteristic was measured using a ball-on-flat tribometer under normal loads of 5, 10, and 15 N. The worn surfaces were characterized by profilometer, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX). PETG/1hBN showed the lowest coefficient of friction (COF) at all tested loads and provided a 40–46% reduction compared to neat PETG. In addition, it was observed to have the wear track with the lowest depth and the smoothest surface. Furthermore, the highest compressive yield strength among the investigated compositions was reached in these specimens. For specimens containing higher h-BN contents, a proportional improvement could not be achieved, and this was interpreted as being due to the agglomeration of the filler material reducing its effectiveness in the transfer film layer. These results show that the addition of a low amount of h-BN to PETG is an effective and easily processable method for improving the wear resistance of the PETG matrix.
articles.summary_en: Researchers found that PETG containing 1 wt% hexagonal boron nitride reduced friction by 40–46% versus neat PETG and achieved the highest compressive yield strength among tested formulations. Higher filler concentrations underperformed, likely because agglomeration weakened the transfer film.

articles.title_original: Microstructure-Informed Effective Phase-Field Model for Structural Fracture of Platelet-Reinforced Hyperelastic Composites
articles.title_en: Phase-field model accelerates fracture analysis of hBN-reinforced silicone composites
articles.excerpt_original: Microstructure-resolved phase-field models capture crack–reinforcement interactions in hyperelastic composites, but repeated platelet-scale fracture calculations are costly for structural analysis. This work develops a microstructure-informed effective phase-field model for hexagonal boron nitride (hBN)-reinforced silicone rubber. Fractography supports a predominantly matrix-dominated, reinforcement-deflected fracture idealization and motivates a mechanical-role-separated closure. A finite-strain phase-field branch represents the fracture-active response, while a low-order auxiliary branch represents reinforcement-mediated load transfer. Both contribute to the effective stress and share one phase-field state, but only the tensile energy of the fracture-active branch drives fracture evolution. Four closure parameters are constrained using 33 proportional multiaxial loading paths and the complete pre-peak histories of all four in-plane first Piola–Kirchhoff stress components. A coefficient-separated reconstruction accelerates the offline search, while the spatial phase-field formulation is retained for structural calculations. The identified parameters are frozen and transferred to re-entrant-corner and edge-defect problems and to a separate five-repeat-per-formulation tensile dataset. Eleven of the 12 structural comparisons have pre-peak NRMSE below 3%, with a maximum of 3.732%, and retain the dominant localization patterns. For the 11 cases with complete terminal reference responses, fracture-displacement differences remain within approximately 3%. Experimental peak-normalized pre-peak RMSE ranges from 1.20% to 2.98%. Structural calculations are typically accelerated by about 4–7×, reaching 11.04× in the fastest benchmark. The framework therefore provides a compact, ful
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a microstructure-informed phase-field model for predicting fracture in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN)-reinforced silicone rubber. The model reproduced structural fracture behavior with mostly under-3% pre-peak error while accelerating calculations by about 4–7×, reaching 11.04× in one benchmark.

articles.title_original: Phonon-Assisted Photoluminescence and Ultrafast Exciton Dynamics in Two-Dimensional Silicon Carbide
articles.title_en: Phonon-Assisted Exciton Dynamics Studied in 2D Silicon Carbide
articles.excerpt_original: Phonon-assisted photoluminescence provides a direct window into exciton-phonon interactions in semiconductors. Using fully ab initio many-body perturbation theory, including finite-momentum Bethe-Salpeter calculations, we investigate phonon-assisted emission and exciton dynamics in two-dimensional (2D) hexagonal silicon carbide (h-SiC) and benchmark its response against 2D h-boron nitride (h-BN). By explicitly resolving exciton-phonon matrix elements, we identify an electron-phonon scattering channel mediated by \({{\rm{E}}}^{{\prime} }\) high-energy longitudinal and transverse optical phonons as the dominant contributors to sideband formation and quantify their spectral weights. We find that h-SiC exhibits pronounced phonon-assisted sidebands comparable to h-BN, despite a smaller exciton-phonon energy separation and fewer resolved replicas. The bright K - K exciton governs both the near-UV zero-phonon emission and the phonon-assisted sidebands through symmetry-allowed longitudinal and transverse optical-phonon coupling. Temperature-dependent scattering rates reveal an ultrashort bright-exciton lifetime of approximately 300 fs at 10 K, highlighting rapid exciton relaxation driven by intrinsic phonon channels.
articles.summary_en: Ab initio many-body calculations show that phonon-assisted emission in two-dimensional hexagonal silicon carbide is dominated by high-energy optical phonon coupling. The work reports ultrafast bright-exciton relaxation, with a lifetime of approximately 300 femtoseconds at 10 K, and benchmarks the material against hexagonal boron nitride.

articles.title_original: First-Principles Study on the Electronic and Mechanical Properties of 2D C 6 H 4 and Its 1D Derivative
articles.title_en: Study Proposes Wide-Bandgap 2D Hydrocarbon Semiconductor
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors with wide bandgaps and robust stability are essential for next-generation electronic devices. Herein, leveraging the stackability of 2D materials, we constructed a novel carbon-hydrogen monolayer material, o -C 6 H 4 . Our first-principles calculations reveal that it exhibits excellent thermal stability, a high Young's modulus, and a negative Poisson's ratio. o -C 6 H 4 is identified as a wide-bandgap semiconductor with a bandgap of 4.03 eV. Ideal tensile tests show that the critical strains along the a-axis, b-axis, and biaxial directions are 0.17, 0.145, and 0.155, respectively, and its mechanical failure is dominated by elastic instability rather than phonon softening. Furthermore, inspired by the ideal tensile results, we explored one-dimensional nanowires (1D-C6H4) derived from the o -C 6 H 4 parent phase and systematically characterized their stability and electronic behavior. This work not only introduces a promising 2D/1D hydrocarbon system but also provides a viable strategy for designing low-dimensional carbon-based semiconductors.
articles.summary_en: First-principles calculations identify o-C6H4 as a thermally stable 2D semiconductor with a 4.03 eV bandgap, high stiffness, and negative Poisson’s ratio. The study also models stable 1D nanowires derived from the material, suggesting a potential platform for low-dimensional carbon-based electronics.

articles.title_original: Characterization of nonlinear dynamics in semiconductors in frequency domain using modulated photoexcitation
articles.title_en: Frequency-Domain Method Characterizes Nonlinear Semiconductor Dynamics
articles.excerpt_original: Carrier dynamics in semiconductors is inherently complex owing to the coexistence of different excited species, such as free carriers and excitons, and their interactions among themselves and with traps and phonons. It is usual to use time-resolved responses to identify the processes that contribute to the dynamics. However, the responses often are non-exponential, leading to ambiguity in the interpretation. Here, we propose a frequency-domain method to characterize nonlinear dynamics in semiconductors using cadmium selenide as the test system. We show that by analyzing the frequency components in the total photoluminescence induced by a pair of phase-modulated beams, the parameters, such as rates of different types of recombination of free carriers and excitons, can be evaluated. The method can be used as a simple diagnostic tool to characterize ultrafast processes that are relevant to the functionality of semiconductor devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers propose a frequency-domain technique to evaluate carrier and exciton recombination rates in cadmium selenide using phase-modulated photoexcitation. The method could provide a simpler diagnostic for ultrafast processes relevant to semiconductor-device functionality.

articles.title_original: Milliampere‐Level p‐Type 2D Zero Differential Transconductance‐MVL Device via Asymmetric Acceptor Doping
articles.title_en: Cl-Doped WSe₂ Device Enables High-Current Ternary Logic
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT The limited performance of p‐type devices, which remain significantly inferior to their n‐type counterparts, is a critical bottleneck in advancing 2D transition‐metal dichalcogenide (2D TMDC)‐based complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) technology. Moreover, in the context of high‐density integration, multivalued logic (MVL) has emerged as a promising approach to reduce device count and interconnect complexity. However, the development of high‐performance p‐type devices for MVL applications remains largely unexplored. Here, we report an asymmetric Cl doping‐induced high‐performance p‐type zero‐differential transconductance (ZDT)‐based MVL device. The facile one‐pot asymmetric Cl doping in vertically stacked WSe 2 channels realizes ternary behavior with three distinct states with a flat middle state within a single device. Owing to the significant efficiency of Cl doping, the resulting p‐type ZDT‐MVL device shows a high on‐current of 1.49 mA. In addition, the Cl‐doped p‐type FET exhibits a low subthreshold swing (SS) of 74.17 mV dec −1 and achieves a high on‐current of 2.83 mA within distinct configurations, respectively. This effective strategy not only achieves high‐performance p‐type characteristics comparable to those of an n‐type FET but also enables the realization of the first 2D TMDC‐based p‐type ZDT‐MVL device, thereby providing a viable platform for CMOS‐based MVL systems.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated a p-type zero-differential-transconductance multivalued-logic device using asymmetric chlorine-doped, vertically stacked WSe₂ channels. The device achieved ternary operation, a 1.49 mA on-current, and a 74.17 mV dec⁻¹ subthreshold swing, supporting potential 2D CMOS and high-density logic applications.

articles.title_original: Magneto-optical Kerr spectroscopy of exciton Rydberg states in a magnetic van der Waals heterostructure
articles.title_en: Kerr spectroscopy probes exciton Rydberg states in magnetic MoSe₂ heterostructure
articles.excerpt_original: Excitonic states in two-dimensional semiconductors are sensitive to time-reversal symmetry breaking, yet how interfacial exchange acts on higher-lying exciton Rydberg states remains largely unexplored. Here we show that wavelength-resolved magneto-optical Kerr spectroscopy of a proximity-coupled MoSe$_2$/Fe$_3$GaTe$_2$ van der Waals heterostructure resolves magnetic symmetry breaking across the A- and B-exciton manifolds. Combining reflection, photoluminescence, and photoluminescence excitation spectroscopy with first-principles many-body calculations including screening by the metallic Fe$_3$GaTe$_2$ layer, we assign the strongly enhanced Kerr resonances to the ground and 2s states of both manifolds. Reversing the magnetic field inverts the polarity of every resonance. A field-odd/field-even decomposition confirms a magnetic origin. The opposite Kerr polarities of the A- and B-exciton manifolds can be explained by proximity-induced exchange coupling to the opposite valence-band spins of the two exciton series. Our results establish resonant Kerr spectroscopy as a sensitive probe of magnetically induced symmetry breaking across the excitonic manifold.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used wavelength-resolved magneto-optical Kerr spectroscopy to resolve magnetic symmetry breaking in the A- and B-exciton manifolds of a MoSe₂/Fe₃GaTe₂ van der Waals heterostructure. The findings identify ground and 2s exciton states and establish resonant Kerr spectroscopy as a sensitive probe of proximity-induced exchange coupling.

articles.title_original: Transport of indirect excitons and exciton mediated spin transport in a van der Waals heterostructure in magnetic fields
articles.title_en: Long-Range Exciton Spin Transport Demonstrated in MoSe₂/WSe₂ Heterostructures
articles.excerpt_original: We studied transport of indirect excitons (IXs) and IX mediated spin transport in a MoSe2/WSe2 van der Waals heterostructure in magnetic fields up to 8 T. We observed long-range IX transport and long-range IX mediated spin transport in magnetic fields. Both IX transport and spin transport are characterized by 1/e decay distances reaching ∼100 μm. The decay distance of spin transport correlates with the decay distance of IX transport. These decay distances first increase and then decrease with increasing IX density for all studied magnetic fields.
articles.summary_en: Researchers observed indirect-exciton transport and exciton-mediated spin transport over decay distances of approximately 100 μm in a MoSe₂/WSe₂ van der Waals heterostructure under magnetic fields up to 8 T. Both transport modes varied non-monotonically with exciton density, highlighting potential for spin-based semiconductor devices.

articles.title_original: Graphene-based photodetector with engineered hot-carrier cooling dynamics
articles.title_en: Proximity Screening Boosts Graphene Photodetector Response by 50%
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Graphene has emerged as a promising material for integration into silicon photonics, owing to its ultrafast and broadband photoresponse without the need for an external bias voltage. This photoresponse relies on the photo-thermoelectric effect created by hot carriers. A key factor underlying the performance of graphene photodetectors is the cooling dynamics of these hot carriers. In this work, we engineer these dynamics in a WSe 2 –graphene–WSe 2 waveguide-integrated photodetector. In particular, by introducing proximity screening by a nearby graphite layer to this structure, we prolong the hot-carrier cooling time, leading to an enhanced photoresponse. We characterize the cooling dynamics under continuous-wave laser excitation by employing a photomixing technique, revealing an increase in the cooling time by up to a factor of four. Direct photoresponse measurements show that the internal photoresponsivity improves by approximately 50%. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of proximity screening to enhance the performance of graphene-based photodetectors on an integrated photonics platform.
articles.summary_en: Researchers engineered hot-carrier cooling in a WSe₂–graphene–WSe₂ waveguide-integrated photodetector using a nearby graphite layer. The approach increased cooling time by up to fourfold and improved internal photoresponsivity by approximately 50%, supporting integrated silicon photonics applications.

articles.title_original: Synergistic Integration of Two-Dimensional Materials and Perovskites for Next-Generation Solar Cells
articles.title_en: Review Highlights Graphene–Perovskite Solar-Cell Integration
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The integration of two-dimensional (2D) materials with metal halide perovskites offers a multidimensional approach for simultaneously addressing the interfacial, electronic, ionic, and stability-related limitations of conventional perovskite solar cells. Despite demonstrating the power conversion efficiencies of over 26%, their practical commercialization remains hindered by factors such as severe environmental instability, ion migration, interfacial recombination, and thermal degradation. Recent studies demonstrate that graphene, transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), MXenes, layered 2D perovskites, and related architectures can modify charge transfer, interfacial energetics, defect populations, crystallization behavior, and ionic transport through cooperative interfacial effects. This review highlights the recent progress in multidimensional 2D-perovskite heterostructures by focusing on interfacial engineering, charge-transfer dynamics, defect passivation mechanisms, and performance-enhancement pathways. There is particular emphasis on graphene-assisted transport layers, TMD-based heterointerfaces, MXene-enabled architectures, graded quasi-2D systems, and van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures. Furthermore, the review also addresses the challenges associated with synthesizing these solar cells, such as scalability, phase instability, interfacial reconstruction, and long-term reliability under operational conditions. The review concludes by discussing promising opportunities in flexible photovoltaics, tandem solar cells, and multifunctional optoelectronic systems. Collectively, synergistic 2D-perovskite heterostructures exhibit a promising route to more efficient, stable, and commercially viable next-generation solar-energy technologies. This review integrates
articles.summary_en: An ACS review examines how graphene and other two-dimensional materials address interfacial recombination, ion migration, instability, and transport limitations in metal-halide perovskite solar cells. It identifies scalable synthesis, phase stability, and long-term reliability as key barriers to commercialization, while highlighting flexible and tandem photovoltaics as opportunities.

articles.source: World Scientific Pub Co Pte Ltd
articles.title_original: Two-Dimensional Materials for Electrochemical Energy Storage, Thermal Energy Storage and Management, and Hydrogen Production and Storage
articles.title_en: Review Identifies Key Translation Challenges for 2D Materials in Energy and Hydrogen Systems
articles.excerpt_original: Two-dimensional (2D) materials combine atomic-scale thickness, open interfaces, and tunable electronic structures, but their practical value depends on whether nanoscale advantages survive processing, assembly, and operation. This review establishes a structure-interface-transport-stability (SITS) framework to compare 2D materials across electrochemical energy storage, thermal energy storage and management, and hydrogen production and storage. This review mainly covers advances since 2021, while retaining selected foundational references needed to establish key concepts, benchmark properties, and mechanistic context. Rather than cataloging materials by application, the analysis examines how common strategies—including thinning, defect engineering, interlayer expansion, functionalization, and heterostructure construction—alter the transport of electrons, ions, phonons, H*, molecular H2, and atomic hydrogen in hydrides. Cross-field comparison reveals a recurring trade-off: strategies that improve site accessibility or local transport often reduce density, increase interfacial resistance, or compromise stability. The central bottleneck is therefore the translation of favorable material-level metrics into reproducible device- and system-level performance. The review identifies 2D materials as most effective when they regulate critical interfaces, sustain continuous transport networks, or integrate complementary functions, and outlines priorities in scalable synthesis, operando validation, multiphysics modeling, and sustainable manufacturing.
articles.summary_en: A review applies a structure-interface-transport-stability framework to assess 2D materials for electrochemical and thermal energy storage, thermal management, and hydrogen production and storage. It highlights trade-offs between transport, accessibility, density, interfacial resistance, and stability, emphasizing scalable synthesis and device-level validation as priorities.

articles.title_original: Low-Dimensional Materials: From Size Confinement to AI-Driven Materials Design Strategy
articles.title_en: Review Surveys Low-Dimensional Materials and AI-Driven Design
articles.excerpt_original: Low-dimensional materials are systems in which one or more characteristic dimensions are restricted to the atomic or nanometer scale [...]
articles.summary_en: The MDPI review examines low-dimensional materials, emphasizing how size confinement influences their properties. It also discusses AI-driven strategies for designing and discovering these materials.

articles.title_original: Gamma Alumina@Boron Nitride Fiber‐Reinforced Functional Composites With Thermal Conductive Networks Exhibiting High Thermal Conductivity and Electrical Insulation
articles.title_en: BN@Alumina Fiber–Epoxy Composites Deliver High Thermal Conductivity and Electrical Insulation
articles.excerpt_original: Functional composites with high thermal conductivity and insulating properties have emerged as a current research hotspot. This study fabricated a novel core–shell structured fiber filler (hexagonal boron nitride@gamma alumina (BN@AO)) using electrospinning technology and produced BN@AO/epoxy resin (EP) composites through hot pressing method. BN@AO filler can form thermal conductive (TC) network in the composites. Microscopically, h‐BN forms a continuous TC path in the BN@AO fibers, and macroscopically, the BN@AO fibers with high aspect ratios can form TC paths directly in the EP matrix. The results show that the optimal in‐plane and out‐of‐plane thermal conductivity ( λ ) of BN@AO/EP are 8.776 and 0.911 W·m −1 ·K −1 at 30 wt% filler loading, which are 3571.96% and 408.93% higher than EP, respectively. Furthermore, the BN@AO/EP composites retain excellent electrical insulation properties, with an AC breakdown field strength exceeding 50 kV·mm −1 . This research presents a fabrication method for high thermal conductivity insulating fillers, applicable to heat dissipation solutions in modern electric and electronic devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers fabricated hexagonal boron nitride@gamma alumina fiber fillers and incorporated them into epoxy composites, achieving thermal conductivity of 8.776 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ in-plane and 0.911 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ through-plane at 30 wt% loading. The composites also retained electrical insulation, indicating potential for heat dissipation in electronic devices.

articles.title_original: Advanced Piezoelectric Nanogenerators for Next-Generation Self-Powered Nano-Bio Sensors
articles.title_en: Review Surveys 2D-Material Piezoelectric Nanogenerators for Self-Powered Biosensors
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Two-dimensional (2D) material-based piezoelectric nanogenerators (PENGs) are emerging as efficient energy-harvesting devices that convert mechanical stimuli into electrical energy. Owing to their tunable electronic, mechanical, and structural characteristics, 2D materials, including TMDs, MXenes, h-BN, etc., offer significant advantages in flexibility, durability, and low-power operation, making them highly suitable for next-generation self-powered systems. This review systematically highlights recent advances in 2D material-based PENGs, emphasizing fabrication strategies, performance optimization, electromechanical coupling enhancement, and their applications in self-powered nano-biosensors. The interdependence between material properties, device architecture, and measurement conditions is comprehensively analyzed to establish robust structure-performance relationships. Furthermore, critical challenges, including low output power, signal instability, integration complexity, and the lack of standardized evaluation protocols, are systematically analyzed. Emerging strategies to enhance energy-harvesting efficiency, signal reliability, and device scalability are also highlighted. Overall, this review establishes a unified framework for the rational design and advancement of high-performance 2D PENGs, providing key insights for their practical implementation in portable, wearable, and autonomous self-powered systems.
articles.summary_en: The review examines fabrication, performance optimization, and electromechanical coupling in 2D-material piezoelectric nanogenerators for wearable and autonomous biosensors. It identifies low output power, signal instability, integration complexity, and inconsistent evaluation standards as key barriers to deployment.

articles.title_original: Defects in graphene
articles.title_en: Engineering and Measuring Defects in Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Zweidimensionale Materialien haben einzigartige Eigenschaften, die sich stark von ihren dreidimensionalen Pendants unterscheiden, wodurch sie auch seit ihrer Entdeckung vor ungefähr zwei Jahrzehnten kontinuierlich großes wissenschaftliches Interesse bewahren konnten. Neben den Bestrebungen zur Synthese immer neuerer atomar dünner Kristalle, bieten bereits bestehende zweidimensionale Materialien ein breites Forschungsgebiet im Rahmen der Manipulation der atomaren Struktur zur Hervorbringung neuer Eigenschaften. Dementsprechend sind sowohl die Synthese neuer zweidimensionaler Festkörper sowie deren Kontrolle auf atomarer Ebene von besonderem Interesse. In dieser Forschungsarbeit wird die atomare Struktur von freistehendem, defektfreiem, einlagigem Graphen durch Ionenbestrahlung im Ultrahochvakuum gezielt manipuliert. Die dafür benötigten anfangs defektfreien einlagigen Regionen werden mittels Ramanspektroskopie lokalisiert, während mehrlagige oder intrinsisch defektreiche Bereiche ausgeschlossen werden. Die durch Ionenbestrahlung manipulierte atomare Struktur wird mittels halbautomatisierter Rastertransmissionselektronenmikroskopie über mesoskopische Flächen abgebildet. Die dadurch entstehenden großen Datensätze werden mittels eines neuronalen Netzes anhand ihrer atomaren Struktur charakterisiert. Dadurch ergibt sich eine statistische Verteilung sowie Flächendichte der erzeugen Defekte. Anschließend wird die atomare Struktur des defektreichen Graphens mit seiner mechanischen Festigkeit, welche durch Rasterkraftmikroskopie Nanoindentierung gemessen wird, korreliert. Diese Korrelation wird erst durch das durchgehende Ultrahochvakuum ermöglicht, welche Luftexposition der Probe und dadurch Veränderung der manipulierten atomaren Struktur zwischen den Messungen an verschiedenen
articles.summary_en: Researchers deliberately introduced defects into pristine monolayer graphene using ion irradiation under ultrahigh vacuum. Raman spectroscopy, automated scanning transmission electron microscopy, neural-network analysis, and atomic-force-microscopy nanoindentation were used to quantify defects and correlate them with mechanical strength.

articles.title_original: Probing tunable Kerr nonlinearity in graphene Josephson junctions
articles.title_en: Graphene Josephson Junctions Demonstrate Tunable Kerr Nonlinearity
articles.excerpt_original: Josephson junction (JJ) is a key nonlinear element in superconducting devices such as qubits, amplifiers, and bolometers. Recently, gate-tunable JJs based on graphene and semiconductors have gained interest due to their rich Andreev physics and wide applications in circuit quantum electrodynamics devices. In addition to gate tunability, it offers many advantages over conventional JJs, such as exceptional thermal properties for bolometric sensors, magnetic-field compatibility, and operability at elevated temperatures above 1 K. Like conventional Al–AlOx–Al JJs, graphene JJs also act as nonlinear inductors, and at their heart lies the Kerr nonlinearity. Additionally, in graphene JJs, the nonlinearity is tunable via external knobs in a single device. However, a detailed experimental exploration of the tunable Kerr nonlinearity in graphene JJs has never been performed. In this work, we study the dependence of the Kerr nonlinearity on gate voltage, temperature, and DC bias—an interesting knob that has been less explored. Using these parameters, we show that the magnitude of the Kerr coefficient can be tuned over a wide range, from ∼200 kHz to 1.2 MHz. Our work will be a valuable resource for further understanding of the nonlinearity in graphene JJs and for the design of next-generation amplifiers and sensors, with enhanced performance.
articles.summary_en: Researchers show that graphene Josephson junctions can tune Kerr nonlinearity from approximately 200 kHz to 1.2 MHz through gate voltage, temperature, and DC bias. The results support potential use in quantum circuits, amplifiers, and bolometric sensors.

articles.title_original: Molecularly engineered boron nitride nanosheet nanofluids with Rayleigh-Bénard-type convection for medium-temperature direct absorption solar collection
articles.title_en: Engineered Boron Nitride Nanofluids Improve Solar-Thermal Collection
articles.excerpt_original: Medium-temperature direct absorption solar collectors (DASCs) remain limited by insufficient optical absorption, poor heat transfer, and inadequate long-term stability of the working fluid. Here, few-layer hexagonal boron nitride nanosheets were coated with polydopamine (PDA) and further grafted with tetradecanamine (TDA) to produce an oil dispersible BNNS@PDA-TDA nanofluid. The PDA layer provided broadband solar absorption, whereas TDA grafting enabled surfactant-free dispersion in heat-transfer oil. The resulting nanofluid increased thermal conductivity by up to 16.7 % relative to the base oil, with only a minor viscosity increase. Optical experiments and FDTD simulations showed that PDA coating dominated the absorption enhancement, while nanosheet thinning reduced scattering and improved the absorption ratio. Under simulated solar irradiation, reverse irradiation established a buoyancy-unstable thermal field and promoted Rayleigh-Bénard-type convection, producing a more uniform temperature field and a maximum photothermal conversion efficiency of 69.52 % at 40 ppm. The nanofluid also exhibited smaller transmittance changes and more reproducible temperature responses during cyclic heating under reverse irradiation than under forward irradiation. These results show that interfacial molecular engineering combined with irradiation-direction control can yield stable, high-efficiency nanofluids suitable for medium-temperature DASC applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed polydopamine- and tetradecanamine-functionalized boron nitride nanosheet nanofluids that increased thermal conductivity by up to 16.7% while remaining dispersible in heat-transfer oil. The fluid achieved a reported photothermal conversion efficiency of 69.52% under simulated solar irradiation, supporting medium-temperature direct absorption solar collectors.

articles.title_original: Tensile-strain-engineered electron–phonon coupling for high-performance n -MoS2/ p -Si photodetector
articles.title_en: Strain Engineering Improves MoS2/Si Photodetector Performance
articles.excerpt_original: Strain induced in multilayered molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) opens a new avenue for carrier dynamics, enabling the development of high-performance optoelectronic devices, including photodetectors. The strong electron–phonon coupling (EPC) can be effectively modulated through intercalation-induced strain engineering. Ion exchange between the intercalant and MoS2 leads to interlayer expansion and lattice distortion, providing an effective route to modulate strain. Hence, here, alkali ion (Mg2+) was initially intercalated in the precursor and subsequently grown on p-Si to n-MoS2/p-Si photodetector, facilitating efficient charge transfer. The redshift of E2g1 and A1g Raman modes in n-MoS2/p-Si indicated the presence of tensile strain, which weakens the EPC in the intercalated MoS2 layer. This strain-induced suppression of the EPC enhances the carrier mobility by approximately 2.6 times and reduces the carrier transit time to about one-fourth of that in the pristine structure. These synergic characteristics make n-MoS2/p-Si an excellent photodetector with fast response and good recovery of 0.9 s (photocyclability) over five cycles and good responsivity of 0.31 A/W. In addition to this, the external quantum efficiency of about 37% is observed for the fabricated photodetector.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used magnesium-ion intercalation to induce tensile strain in multilayer MoS2, weakening electron–phonon coupling and increasing carrier mobility by approximately 2.6 times. The resulting n-MoS2/p-Si photodetector achieved 0.31 A/W responsivity, approximately 37% external quantum efficiency, and 0.9-second photocyclability response and recovery.

articles.title_original: Reconstructive Polarimetry With Scalable Graphene–Metal Infrared Photodetectors
articles.title_en: Scalable Graphene–Metal Photodetectors Enable Infrared Polarimetry
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Recent advent of smart photodetectors, where in situ tuning of responsivity enables the reconstruction of light intensity, polarization, and spectrum by a single device, has revolutionized the field of optoelectronics. So far, most such reconstructive detectors were realized with non‐scalable technology of van der Waals stacking. Here, we demonstrate the infrared reconstructive polarimetry with photodetectors based on conventional gated graphene–metal junctions. The reconstruction exploits the gate tuning of polarization contrast, which enables the determination of both infrared power and polarization angle from photovoltage measurements at two different gate voltages. The physics enabling the polarimetry lies in polarization‐dependent shift of the electron hot spot near the contact, and the gate tuning of photosensitive barrier width. We further show the universality of polarization reconstruction, i.e. its feasibility with different geometries of the junction, and with graphene of different quality, from boron–nitride encapsulated flakes to the scalable chemical vapor deposited films.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate infrared power and polarization reconstruction using gated graphene–metal junction photodetectors, avoiding non-scalable van der Waals stacking. The approach works across junction geometries and graphene qualities, including scalable chemical-vapor-deposited films.

articles.title_original: Graphene Oxide Formation Mechanism and Organosulfates Interlayer Bridging
articles.title_en: Study clarifies graphene oxide formation and sulfate interlayer bridging
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT A kinetic investigation of graphite oxidation using a modified Hummers method was conducted to clarify the structural evolution of graphene oxide (GO) and the formation of sulfur‐containing functionalities. Graphite was oxidized for 2, 12, and 28 h, producing graphite oxides referred to as GrO‐2 h, GrO‐12 h, and GrO‐28 h. Structural and chemical characterization was performed using xX‐ray diffraction (XRD), Raman spectroscopy, atomic force microscopy (AFM), X‐ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), solid‐state 13 C NMR (SSNMR), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and energy‐dispersive spectroscopy (EDS). The results showed that prolonged oxidation did not significantly increase the oxidation degree but instead promoted defect formation, sulfur incorporation, and structural reorganization. Experimental evidence suggests that sulfate/organosulfate species are introduced during the early stages of oxidation and may subsequently participate in interlayer interactions, potentially involving sulfate‐bridging configurations between GO sheets. A mechanistic model based on nucleophilic substitution reactions is proposed to describe the formation of hydroxyl, epoxide, and sulfate functionalities during graphite oxidation. These findings provide new insights into the kinetics of GO formation and contribute to improved control over GO synthesis.
articles.summary_en: A kinetic study of modified-Hummers oxidation finds that longer reaction times primarily increase defect formation, sulfur incorporation, and structural reorganization rather than oxidation degree. The proposed sulfate/organosulfate interlayer interactions and reaction mechanism could support tighter control of graphene oxide synthesis.

articles.title_original: Investigation of Graphene-Based Nanomaterials for Advanced Electronic Applications
articles.title_en: Framework Evaluates Graphene Nanomaterials for Advanced Electronics
articles.excerpt_original: Graphene-based nanomaterials combine atomic-scale thickness with high carrier mobility, tunable electrostatic response, mechanical flexibility, optical transparency, and large current-carrying capability, making them attractive for high-frequency transistors, transparent electrodes, sensors, and other emerging electronic systems. This methodology paper establishes a reproducible framework for investigating how synthesis quality, structural defects, dimensional confinement, and device geometry influence electronic performance. The proposed workflow integrates chemical vapor deposition (CVD) growth on copper, polymer-assisted transfer to Si/SiO2 substrates, Raman and atomic-force-microscopy characterization, lithographic formation of graphene field-effect transistor (GFET) or nanoribbon channels, and current-voltage/gate-voltage measurements. Primary response variables are sheet resistance, charge-neutrality voltage, field-effect mobility, current on/off ratio, and, for confined structures, effective transport gap. A literature-bounded demonstration dataset is used only to show how the analytical pipeline operates; it is not presented as newly measured experimental data. The framework is designed to distinguish conductivity-oriented applications, where pristine large-area graphene is preferred, from switching applications, where controlled band-gap opening through nanostructuring or bilayer electrostatics is required. The study concludes that graphene is especially compelling for radio-frequency, transparent, sensing, and interconnect functions, while its zero-band gap remains a central limitation for conventional digital logic.
articles.summary_en: The academic study proposes a reproducible workflow linking graphene synthesis quality, defects, dimensional confinement, and device geometry to electronic performance. It targets transistors, transparent electrodes, sensors, and interconnects, while identifying graphene’s zero band gap as a limitation for conventional digital logic.

articles.title_original: Optical and Electrical Properties of Graphene-Based Nanostructures
articles.title_en: Computational Framework Maps Graphene Nanostructure Optical and Electrical Properties
articles.excerpt_original: Graphene-based nanostructures combine the exceptional carrier transport of two-dimensional graphene with size-, edge-, and doping-dependent electronic and optical responses. This methodology paper develops a compact computational framework for studying pristine graphene, graphene nanoribbons, and graphene quantum dots using a nearest-neighbor tight-binding description, Kubo-type optical conductivity, and Landauer electrical transport. The procedure defines atomistic geometries, calculates energy bands and density of states, evaluates optical transition spectra, and estimates conductance while systematically varying ribbon width, edge configuration, quantum-dot size, and Fermi-level position. Validation is anchored to well-established observations including the approximately 2.3% visible-light absorbance of monolayer graphene, width-dependent band-gap opening in nanoribbons, and tunable optical transitions in confined graphene structures [2-4,9-14]. Representative model results show that lateral confinement opens a band gap in armchair nanoribbons, shifts the first optical transition to higher energy as dimensions decrease, and suppresses low-bias conductance near charge neutrality. Electrostatic doping, in contrast, preserves the zero-gap character of extended graphene while changing intraband conductivity and suppressing low-energy interband transitions through Pauli blocking. The proposed methodology is suitable for comparative design studies of graphene optoelectronic structures before more expensive density-functional or many-body calculations are performed.
articles.summary_en: A tight-binding, Kubo conductivity, and Landauer transport framework models pristine graphene, nanoribbons, and quantum dots. Results show confinement-dependent band gaps and optical shifts, while doping tunes conductivity without opening a gap in extended graphene, supporting early-stage optoelectronic design.

articles.title_original: Computational Study of Electronic Band Structures in Graphene-Based Nanomaterials
articles.title_en: Computational Framework for Graphene Electronic Band Structures
articles.excerpt_original: Graphene-based nanomaterials are attractive for nanoelectronic, optoelectronic, sensing, and thermoelectric applications because their electronic states can be modified by lateral confinement, edge geometry, chemical substitution, strain, and structural defects. This methodology paper presents a reproducible computational framework for examining electronic band structures in pristine graphene and graphene-derived nanostructures using a two-level strategy: a nearest-neighbor tight-binding model for rapid physical validation and density functional theory (DFT) for atomistic refinement. The workflow defines structural model construction, vacuum separation, geometry optimization, Brillouin-zone sampling, band-path calculations, density-of-states analysis, and convergence criteria. A tight-binding calculation carried out for pristine graphene reproduces the characteristic crossing of valence and conduction bands at the K point, giving a zero-band gap in the ideal sheet. The interpretation of nanoribbon, doped, strained, and defected systems is then benchmarked against peer-reviewed studies published no later than 2017. The literature demonstrates that lateral confinement and edge effects can open band gaps in graphene nanoribbons, while B/N substitution, strain, and defects shift or reshape states near the Fermi level. The proposed protocol therefore provides a compact and defensible route for comparing electronic-structure changes across graphene-based nanomaterials while preserving computational efficiency and methodological transparency.
articles.summary_en: Researchers present a reproducible workflow combining tight-binding calculations and density functional theory to analyze electronic structures in pristine and modified graphene nanomaterials. The methodology examines how confinement, doping, strain, and defects alter band gaps and electronic states, supporting research in semiconductor, sensing, and optoelectronic applications.

articles.title_original: Graphene-Enhanced Magnetic Anisotropies in Fe/Ni (100) Superlattices with Monolayer Periodicity
articles.title_en: Graphene Tunes Magnetic Anisotropy in Fe/Ni Superlattices
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Fe/Ni(100) superlattices grown on graphene/Ir(100) by intercalation of alternate monolayers of Ni and Fe under graphene show magnetic properties severely modified. The graphene–iron interaction at the external interface produces a surface anisotropy Kint(gr/Fe) = 0.89 ± 0.08 mJ/m2, large enough to drive the uniaxial, out-of-plane magnetic anisotropy of the whole superlattice to KU = 0.87 ± 0.03 MJ/m3 and compensate the in-plane shape anisotropy characteristic of thin magnetic layers. Graphene also introduces an additional trigonal in-plane anisotropy superimposed to the biaxial anisotropy of the underlying Fe/Ni (100) superlattice and increases the mL(parallel)/mspin ratio by 50% with respect to Fe/Ni films grown without graphene, as determined by XMCD. The films show chemical ordering plane-by-plane and a strongly distorted face-centered tetragonal (fct) structure, as determined by synchrotron-based X-ray diffraction. The gr-Fe charge transfer and the electronic hybridization of the respective π and d bands at the interface are responsible for the observed magnetic phenomena.
articles.summary_en: Researchers show that graphene interfaces substantially modify the magnetic anisotropy of monolayer-periodic Fe/Ni(100) superlattices, producing strong out-of-plane anisotropy and an additional trigonal component. Charge transfer and π–d orbital hybridization at the graphene–iron interface are identified as the mechanisms.

articles.title_original: Structural Role of Different MXenes in CoMnS Composites for High-Energy Ionic Liquid Supercapacitors
articles.title_en: MXene–CoMnS Composites Boost Ionic-Liquid Supercapacitor Performance
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract A systematic comparative study of three MXenes, Ti3C2 (TC), V2C (VC), and Mo2Ti2C3 (MTC), and their corresponding CoMnS (CMS) composites was conducted to elucidate the influence of MXene chemistry on electrochemical performance. The composites were synthesized via in situ growth of CMS on MXene surfaces, promoting strong interfacial interactions and uniform dispersion of redox-active species. Structural characterization revealed that TC possesses the most ordered layered structure and highest synthesis efficiency, whereas MTC exhibits a more disordered morphology. Despite this, MTC-based composites delivered superior electrochemical performance owing to enhanced interfacial activity and faster ion/electron transport. All MXene/CMS composites significantly outperformed their pristine counterparts when employed as positive electrodes in asymmetric supercapacitors. A maximum energy density of 432.3 Wh kg–1 and a specific capacitance of 1216 F g–1 were achieved by the MTC/CMS device at 0.5 A g–1. The highest power density of 8000 W kg–1 was obtained from the MTC/CMS device at 5 A g–1 current density. In addition, a capacitance retention of ∼94% was observed after 10,000 continuous cycles in an ionic liquid electrolyte. These enhanced properties are credited to a mutual reinforcement between Co/Mn redox-active pseudocapacitance and MXene-derived electric double-layer capacitance. Overall, the electrochemical performance follows the order: MTC/CMS > VC/CMS > TC/CMS > MTC > VC > TC > CMS, highlighting the importance of MXene-dependent interfacial engineering for advanced energy-storage systems.
articles.summary_en: A comparative study found that Mo2Ti2C3-based CoMnS composites delivered the strongest electrochemical performance among the tested MXene systems. The device achieved 432.3 Wh kg−1 energy density, 8,000 W kg−1 power density, and approximately 94% capacitance retention after 10,000 cycles.
